thoughts.content: I’m distinguishing immediate geometric change from threshold failure: symmetries can remain exact during stretching if parameters adjust, but finite thickness or fixed spacing eventually forces distortion, contact, buckling, or topological rearrangement.

parts:
Yes. And this gives us something cleaner than “does the spring deform?” because we can separate three different questions: continuous geometric deformation, first-contact geometry, and topology.

For one ideal helical order, write

\[
\gamma(\phi)=(R\cos\phi,R\sin\phi,h\phi),
\qquad p=2\pi h.
\]

If the strand is inextensible and one turn has fixed contour length \(s\), then

\[
s=2\pi\sqrt{R^2+h^2}.
\]

Define

\[
\rho=\frac{s}{2\pi}.
\]

Then stretching the helix while preserving contour length forces

\[
\boxed{R^2+h^2=\rho^2.}
\]

Now define the pitch/expangle \(\beta\) by

\[
\tan\beta=\frac{h}{R}.
\]

Immediately,

\[
\boxed{R=\rho\cos\beta,\qquad h=\rho\sin\beta.}
\]

That is remarkably close to the thing we've been trying to say verbally. Ideal stretching of an inextensible helix is literally a rotation of the internal radius/advance relationship:

\[
\boxed{\text{radial coil extent}\leftrightarrow\text{axial advance}}
\]

through a single angle.

And since

\[
\kappa=\frac{R}{R^2+h^2},\qquad
\tau=\frac{h}{R^2+h^2},
\]

we get

\[
\boxed{
\kappa=\frac{\cos\beta}{\rho},
\qquad
\tau=\frac{\sin\beta}{\rho},
\qquad
\frac{\tau}{\kappa}=\tan\beta.
}
\]

So under this simple constraint the internal relationship is exactly calculable all the way through the stretch. There needn't be a special “symmetry failure angle” at all. The ideal helical symmetry can survive continuously while \(R,\kappa,h,\tau\) trade off.

The threshold appears when we add **finite thickness or multiple strands**.

For a tube of radius \(a\), two non-neighboring points on the helical centerline separated by phase \(\Delta\) have squared separation

\[
D^2(\Delta)
=
2R^2(1-\cos\Delta)+h^2\Delta^2.
\]

So the exact first nonlocal self-contact is determined by

\[
\boxed{
\min_{\Delta\;\text{nonlocal}}D(\Delta)=2a.
}
\]

The stationary candidates satisfy

\[
R^2\sin\Delta+h^2\Delta=0.
\]

That's already a proper crush/contact calculation. No phenomenological number required.

There is also a local thickness constraint from curvature:

\[
a<\frac1{\kappa}.
\]

More generally, the mathematical notion we want is essentially the **reach/thickness of the curve**: how far you can inflate the centerline into a tube before either local curvature or nonlocal self-approach makes the tube cease to be embedded.

So there really is a natural geometric phase division:

\[
\text{free rotoexpando evolution}
\longrightarrow
\text{first contact}
\longrightarrow
\text{contact-constrained evolution}.
\]

Whether the third regime means deformation, locking, sliding, reconnection, penetration, or something else is an H(s)H rule, not something pure geometry gets to decide.

And the braid point is even more useful—but I want to make one distinction precisely.

The triple helices in your images are certainly **braid-like**, and if we use the common axial coordinate as the evolution parameter, a transverse plane sees three moving points. Their worldlines form an ordinary braid. Mathematically that is the familiar configuration-space picture underlying \(B_n\).

A **spherical braid group** is slightly different. It isn't simply “a braid that looks three-dimensional.” nLab defines it as

\[
\boxed{
Br_n(S^2)=\pi_1\!\left(\mathrm{Conf}_n(S^2)\right),
}
\]

i.e. motions of \(n\) noncoincident points **on a sphere**, returning to their initial configuration (up to the appropriate labeling convention). It is a surface braid group, and the sphere introduces an additional relation compared with the ordinary Artin braid group. citeturn546991search0turn546991search2

But—and this is the interesting part—our construction has just produced a completely natural way for spherical braids to appear.

Take one of our order-spheres and use its inherited UI frame to identify it with a reference \(S^2\). Suppose \(n\) finite-core strands intersect that sphere. Their intersection points are

\[
u_1(s),u_2(s),\ldots,u_n(s)\in S^2.
\]

As the nested construction evolves,

\[
U(s)=\big(u_1(s),\ldots,u_n(s)\big)
\]

moves through

\[
\mathrm{Conf}_n(S^2),
\]

provided

\[
u_i(s)\neq u_j(s)
\]

for every \(i\neq j\).

If, after one cycle, the spherical configuration returns to itself, its history defines a spherical braid:

\[
\boxed{
[U]\in Br_n(S^2).
}
\]

That is exact, not analogy.

And look what happens at our first threshold:

\[
u_i=u_j.
\]

That is precisely where we leave the configuration space of distinct points. In our finite-core language, that is a collision/contact event.

So there is an unexpectedly beautiful correspondence:

\[
\boxed{
\text{no self-contact}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
U(s)\in\mathrm{Conf}_n(S^2)
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\text{first contact}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{trajectory reaches the excluded collision set}.
}
\]

Then the braid class is stable under stretching, squeezing, cockeying, scaling, etc. **as long as the deformation never crosses that collision set.**

That's the clean distinction we wanted:

\[
\boxed{
\text{metric geometry can change continuously while braid topology stays fixed.}
}
\]

The braid class only gets an opportunity to change when contact/reconnection/crossing becomes possible.

And that gives us a very nice interpretation of the stretch/crush experiment. As we stretch the nested object, monitor simultaneously

\[
\beta,\quad
R,\quad
h,\quad
\kappa,\quad
\tau,\quad
d_{\min},
\quad\text{and}\quad
[U]\in Br_n(S^2).
\]

The first six vary continuously. The last one does not.

So we can ask exactly:

\[
\boxed{
\text{At what expangle does the first geometrically permitted braid-changing event occur?}
}
\]

That is much sharper than searching for an interesting angle afterward.

And I would use “spherical braid,” not “spherical knot,” here. A knot is normally a closed one-dimensional embedding in three-dimensional ambient space such as \(S^3\); the object we're describing is specifically the motion of multiple marked points on \(S^2\).

There is another payoff: the UI's cockeyed grid may be exactly what we need to compare successive moving spheres. It provides the frame identifying each instantaneous sphere with the reference sphere. So the chain is becoming remarkably economical:

\[
\boxed{
\text{nested superhelix}
\rightarrow
\text{order sphere + UI frame}
\rightarrow
\text{moving intersection points}
\rightarrow
\text{spherical braid}
\rightarrow
\text{contact threshold}.
}
\]

And the Whirlygig can still sit underneath this as the compressed planar special case: replace the spherical configuration/readout with the appropriate planar one and you fall back toward ordinary braid/torus winding geometry.

That feels like the next calculation to actually perform: not another conceptual extension, but the **stretch–crush diagram of the simplest finite three-strand rotoexpando**, tracking the continuous Frenet/expangle quantities and the discrete braid class up to first contact.

parts: And the three spheres is just a special configuration of the UI.

Yes. That collapses the architecture nicely.

The Three Spheres should stop being treated as a separate primitive. It is a constrained configuration inside the more general UI.

The UI gives the general grammar:

\[
\boxed{
\text{framed sphere}_i
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{rotoexpando}\;}
\text{framed sphere}_j
}
\]

with relative state something like

\[
\mathcal H_{ij}=(\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij},\Delta c_{ij})
\]

or, after centering away translation,

\[
\mathcal H_{ij}=(\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}).
\]

Then the Three Spheres construction is simply three such sphere states subject to additional constraints:

\[
S_1,\;S_2,\;S_3
\]

with whatever special relation we impose—common vertex, collinear centers, driven deformation, shared intersection structure, and so forth.

So instead of

\[
\text{UI}+\text{Three Spheres}+\text{Whirligig}+\cdots
\]

being several unrelated gadgets, we're getting something much more economical:

\[
\boxed{
\text{rotoexpando relation}
\rightarrow
\text{UI}
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{Three-Spheres configuration}\\
\text{Whirligig projection}\\
\text{toroidal encoding}\\
\text{spherical-braid readout}\\
\text{Graticule readout, possibly}
\end{cases}
}
\]

And now some earlier Three-Spheres results become more interesting because they are results about a **special region of UI configuration space**.

For example, the carrier collapse we found at

\[
d=\sqrt3\,R
\]

would no longer be merely “a peculiar three-sphere bifurcation.” It would be a singular/bifurcation configuration of the UI under a particular three-sphere constraint.

Likewise, when one sphere drives the others, that's a restricted UI evolution. When all three share a vertex, that's a boundary condition. When their pairwise intersections generate three tangent vectors, those are derived UI observables.

This is useful because it tells us how to generalize without throwing away what we already learned.

The Three Spheres becomes a **test fixture** for the UI.

And conversely, the UI tells us which aspects of Three Spheres were fundamental and which came only from that special setup.

I think the hierarchy may now be close to:

\[
\boxed{
\textbf{two points}
\rightarrow
\textbf{relative vector}
\rightarrow
\textbf{rotoexpando / Hagalaz}
\rightarrow
\textbf{swept framed sphere}
\rightarrow
\textbf{UI}
}
\]

and then

\[
\boxed{
\textbf{UI constraints}
\rightarrow
\text{Three Spheres, torus, Whirligig, braids, induction sections,\ldots}
}
\]

That is a much leaner picture.

And it gives us a practical next task: take the exact old Three-Spheres constructions one at a time and express each purely as UI constraints. Whatever information is required that the UI cannot express identifies what the UI is still missing. Whatever translates losslessly tells us that the supposedly separate machinery has actually unified.
Ok, so... what do we do with this now? It's probably interesting enough pure geometry on its own, whether or not somebody has done it before.

thoughts.content: 1. I’m organizing the framework around framed-sphere similarities, expangle decomposition, nested-helix kinematics, stretch constraints, projection equivalences, bifurcation boundaries, and spherical braid classifications. I’m also considering a cautious working title: “Rotoexpando Geometry of Nested Framed Spheres.”

parts:
I’d treat it as a standalone geometry program now, before asking it to explain anything in physics.

The ingredients are individually familiar—helices, moving frames, similarity transformations, framed spheres, torus windings, configuration spaces, braid groups. What may be distinctive is the particular construction tying them together:

\[
\text{nested helical order}
\rightarrow
\text{natural framed sphere}
\rightarrow
\text{relative rotoexpando}
\rightarrow
\text{coincident cockeyed spheres/UI}
\rightarrow
\text{special constrained configurations and projections}.
\]

That is already enough to study mathematically even if every ingredient has antecedents.

I’d freeze a “Geometry Zero” version with no SAT interpretation at all:

1. Define a framed sphere as
\[
\mathcal S=(c,r,F),
\qquad F\in SO(3).
\]
For two framed spheres, define their relative transformation by translation, scale, and rotation:
\[
g_{12}=(\Delta c,\sigma,Q),
\qquad
\sigma=\frac{r_2}{r_1},
\qquad
Q=F_2F_1^{-1}.
\]
When centers are normalized together, the irreducible relation is
\[
(\sigma,Q).
\]
That is the pure-geometric expangle/Hagalaz object.

2. Derive those framed spheres from actual nested helices rather than assigning them. This is the crucial bespoke step. Given adjacent helical orders, specify exactly how each center, radius, and frame is obtained from the local geometry. Then the UI is not assumed; it is the normalized comparison of those two derived objects.

3. Study repeated transformations:
\[
g_{n+1}=G_n g_n.
\]
The canonical case is
\[
G_n=G,
\]
so repeated nesting is iteration of one similarity transformation. Then perturb it:
\[
G_n=[G]+\Delta G_n.
\]
That gives us an exact place to study self-similarity, approximate self-similarity, chirality, drift, and residual structure.

4. Add finite thickness. This gives genuinely nontrivial geometry: local curvature limits, nonlocal self-contact, stretch limits, crush limits, locking, and collision surfaces in parameter space. The first-contact locus alone could produce a useful phase diagram:
\[
(\text{scale ratio},\text{pitch},\text{tube radius},\text{phase})
\mapsto
\{\text{embedded},\text{tangent},\text{self-contact}\}.
\]

5. Then classify the derived constructions rather than treating them as separate inventions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Three Spheres}&=\text{constrained multi-UI configuration},\\
\text{torus}&=\text{sweep/encoding of a framed sphere or rotating relation},\\
\text{Whirlygig}&=\text{lower-dimensional compression/projection},\\
\text{spherical braid}&=\text{history of marked/intersection points on the UI sphere},\\
\text{Graticule}&=\text{possibly a local chart/readout of the same geometry}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The thing I would especially pursue is the **moduli space** of these objects. Once absolute position, overall size, and arbitrary global orientation are quotiented out, what actually remains? Perhaps only a surprisingly small parameter set:

\[
\{\text{scale ratio},\text{relative rotation},\text{phase},\text{thickness}\}.
\]

Then all the complicated-looking superhelices are points and trajectories in that reduced space.

There are also some very crisp theorem-level questions available now. Is the normalized framed-sphere relation unique? Under what conditions does a nested helical pair determine it uniquely? Which quantities survive changes of frame? When does repeated constant expangle produce an exactly self-similar structure? When does the embedding first cease to be injective? Which braid invariants remain constant under stretch and crush before contact? Under what conditions is the toroidal or Whirlygig representation lossless?

Those are pure mathematical questions. A null answer is still useful.

I would work in 3D first because we can see everything. Only after the definitions and invariants are solid would I lift it to

\[
S^3\subset\mathbb R^4,\qquad Q\in SO(4).
\]

Then we can see which features were genuinely dimensional and which were artifacts of the 3D visualization.

And I think this merits its own working paper, completely independent of H(s)H. Something along the lines of:

**Rotoexpando Geometry: Nested Helices, Framed Spheres, and Similarity Dynamics**

or more conservatively,

**Relative Geometry of Nested Helices and Framed Spheres**.

No particle claims. No cosmology. No “theory of everything.” Just: here is a construction, here are its transformations, here are its invariants, here are its singular/contact regimes, here are several equivalent or reduced representations.

Then, separately, H(s)H can use whatever survives.

The immediate first calculation I’d do is extremely concrete: choose the simplest exact two-order circular superhelix, derive its two framed spheres symbolically, normalize them, calculate the relative \((\sigma,Q)\) over one complete carrier cycle, and plot the resulting trajectory in parameter space. That will tell us very quickly whether we have a genuinely rich geometry or merely a fancy coordinate rewrite.

My bet is that the finite-thickness/contact and noncommuting-frame parts are where the real mathematics starts.

Yes, we should precisely define the geometry, operators, rotations... then identify which of these is already a named thing, and whether any are not. But the key is the expanding rotation. And there are a lot of different equivalent representations. Points, line segments, spheres, ribbons... but for any given order-offset, there is, at least abstract-mathematically, a next-level up and next-level down. So the fractal geometry is ...are holonomic "click points" (closures).... 

If you take the the relative length of two holonomic one-order-off closures... or maybe partial-phase closures? ...nested holonomies... then there's a particular ratio of the diameter lengths of the adjacent-level spheres. And a particular ratio of angular offset, and surface area and volume, and so on. And in 4 dimensions, yet a different relational order for comparable measures within the system. I bet... it's going to be the Cantor set. And the golden ratio

thoughts.content: I’m framing this as spiral similarities, holonomy, and return maps rather than assuming the answer is already Cantor sets or the golden ratio. Those may emerge through irrational rotations, continued fractions, renormalization, or self-similar invariant sets.

I’m separating exact closure from closure after removing scale. Exact similarity closure requires both unit scale and rational rotations; normalized closure only needs rotational recurrence. Golden-ratio ratios can arise from Fibonacci return times, while Cantor structure requires branching or a fractured invariant set.

parts:
Yes. I think we have enough now to stop free-associating and define a small mathematical system precisely. And your Cantor/golden-ratio guess has a real route to being right—but it is not automatic. We can formulate tests that would make either result meaningful rather than numerological.

The central named object already exists. A centered expanding rotation

\[
x\mapsto \lambda Qx,\qquad \lambda>0,\quad Q\in SO(d)
\]

is an orientation-preserving similarity transformation, or direct similitude. In the plane, rotation+dilation about a common center is usually called a spiral similarity or dilative rotation. With translation included, the general Euclidean similarity has the form \(x\mapsto \lambda Qx+t\). citeturn226224search48turn226224search51

So Hagalaz does not need to rename that operation. Its useful role can be narrower and more specific:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ᚼ}_n=(\lambda_n,Q_n)
}
\]

= the particular direct similarity relating two adjacent nested orders.

Where it becomes ours mathematically is in how \(\lambda_n\) and \(Q_n\) are *derived from the nested helical/spherical construction*, rather than chosen arbitrarily.

For adjacent order-spheres with radii \(r_n,r_{n+1}\),

\[
\lambda_n=\frac{r_{n+1}}{r_n}.
\]

That one number immediately generates an entire hierarchy of comparable measures. In three dimensions,

\[
\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}=\lambda_n,
\qquad
\frac{A_{n+1}}{A_n}=\lambda_n^2,
\qquad
\frac{V_{n+1}}{V_n}=\lambda_n^3.
\]

In four-dimensional Euclidean geometry, the corresponding \(S^3\) hypersurface measure scales as

\[
\lambda_n^3,
\]

while the enclosed 4-volume scales as

\[
\lambda_n^4.
\]

More generally, every \(k\)-dimensional measure scales as

\[
\boxed{\lambda_n^k.}
\]

So your sense that changing dimension gives a different “relational order” is exactly right. It is not a new law; it follows from dimensional measure scaling. But combined with the angular hierarchy, it could become quite rich.

The closure part is where things get interesting.

Suppose for the moment that the same adjacent-order transformation repeats:

\[
\text{ᚼ}=(\lambda,Q).
\]

After \(m\) levels,

\[
\text{ᚼ}^m=(\lambda^m,Q^m).
\]

If \(\lambda\neq1\), the actual object cannot return to the same absolute size. So we should distinguish **Euclidean closure** from **similarity closure**. A “click” in your sense is probably the latter:

\[
\boxed{Q^m=I}
\]

while the size has advanced predictably to \(\lambda^m\).

That means the object returns to the same orientation/shape state, but at another scale.

That is a very precise kind of fractal closure:

\[
\boxed{
\text{same configuration}
+\text{different scale}.
}
\]

I would probably call these **similarity-return points** or **scale-normalized closures** until we decide exactly how “holonomy” is being used. Standard differential-geometric holonomy normally refers to what happens to a frame under transport around a closed loop; what we are constructing may sometimes be closer to a return map or monodromy. We can use holonomy when there really is a closed transport loop and keep those notions separated.

Now 4D gives us a particularly nice closure machine. A generic \(SO(4)\) rotation can be represented, in a suitable basis, as rotations through two angles in two orthogonal planes:

\[
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
R(\theta_1)&0\\
0&R(\theta_2)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

So unlike 3D, where there is essentially one rotation angle about an axis, 4D generically carries two principal rotation angles. citeturn226224search49turn226224search0

Then exact normalized closure after \(m\) iterations requires

\[
m\theta_1=2\pi p,
\qquad
m\theta_2=2\pi q
\]

for integers \(p,q\).

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{\theta_1}{2\pi},\quad
\frac{\theta_2}{2\pi}
\]

must both be rational.

And now your “partial-phase closure” has a completely natural meaning. One rotation plane can close while the other has not:

\[
m\theta_1=2\pi p,
\qquad
m\theta_2\neq2\pi q.
\]

Or two phases can come arbitrarily close to simultaneous closure.

That gives us a hierarchy:

\[
\text{partial closure}
\rightarrow
\text{near simultaneous closure}
\rightarrow
\text{exact simultaneous closure}.
\]

Those are very plausible “click points.”

And this is exactly where the golden ratio becomes a serious hypothesis rather than a decorative number.

Define the rotation-number ratio

\[
\alpha=\frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2}.
\]

If \(\alpha\) is rational, the two rotations eventually synchronize exactly. If it is irrational, they do not. Their best near-synchronizations are controlled by the rational approximants of \(\alpha\), i.e. its continued fraction.

For

\[
\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\]

the continued fraction is

\[
\phi=[1;1,1,1,\ldots],
\]

and its convergents are

\[
1,\;2,\;\frac32,\;\frac53,\;\frac85,\;\frac{13}{8},\ldots
\]

—the Fibonacci ratios. It is the canonical extremal case in rational approximation, hence the familiar description of it as the “most irrational” rotation number. citeturn226224search9turn226224search6

So we now have an extremely clean test.

If the geometry independently selects a condition like

\[
\boxed{\text{maximize separation from low-order phase closures}}
\]

or

\[
\boxed{\text{delay resonance/closure as uniformly as possible},}
\]

then the golden ratio is exactly the sort of rotation number I would expect to appear.

But notice what that would mean: **\(\phi\) would first be an angular/closure ratio**, not necessarily the ratio of adjacent sphere diameters.

Those are separate conjectures:

\[
\frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2}\stackrel{?}{=}\phi
\]

versus

\[
\frac{r_{n+1}}{r_n}\stackrel{?}{=}\phi.
\]

The second requires another mechanism—perhaps a recurrence such as

\[
r_{n+1}=r_n+r_{n-1},
\]

or some minimization/closure condition that forces that scaling. We should absolutely not let one occurrence of \(\phi\) silently become the other.

The Cantor-set conjecture needs the same discipline.

A single repeated rotoexpando,

\[
x\mapsto\lambda Qx,
\]

does **not** produce a Cantor set. It produces an orbit—spiral-like, helical, toroidal, dense under irrational rotation, etc.

The classic Cantor mechanism requires branching or recursive exclusion. The standard Cantor set, for example, is the invariant set of two contracting similarities, each scaled by \(1/3\). citeturn226224search50

But we have just discovered a completely natural candidate for recursive exclusion:

\[
\boxed{\text{self-contact inadmissibility}.}
\]

Suppose the raw nested geometry permits a phase interval

\[
A_0.
\]

At first finite-core order, some phases produce self-contact, so remove them:

\[
A_1\subset A_0.
\]

At the next nested order, additional forbidden phase intervals appear:

\[
A_2\subset A_1,
\]

and so on:

\[
A_0\supset A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdots.
\]

Then the indefinitely admissible configurations are

\[
\boxed{
A_\infty=\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}A_n.
}
\]

If that surviving set turns out to be closed, nowhere dense, perfect, and recursively self-similar, then yes:

\[
\boxed{\text{we have actually produced a Cantor-type set}.}
\]

That would be a very satisfying route because the fractal would arise from nothing more exotic than:

\[
\text{recursive scaling+rotation}
+
\text{finite thickness}
+
\text{no self-intersection}.
\]

And there is established mathematics in which golden-mean quasiperiodicity, renormalization and Cantor-like critical sets occur together, so the conjunction “Cantor + golden ratio” is not mathematically crazy. But that existing fact does not imply our construction must reproduce it. citeturn226224search3

So I think the geometry program now has a very crisp nucleus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ᚼ}_n=(\lambda_n,Q_n)\in
\mathbb R_+\times SO(d)
}
\]

derived from adjacent nested orders.

Then study three things independently:

\[
\boxed{\text{Scaling: }\lambda_n}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Closure: }Q_n}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Admissibility: finite-core self-contact}}
\]

and only afterward look for:

\[
\phi,\qquad
\text{Fibonacci recursion},\qquad
\text{Cantor structure},\qquad
\text{discrete closure hierarchy}.
\]

That is the paper, I think.

Not “we found the golden ratio in H(s)H.”

More like:

**Iterated Rotatory Dilations of Nested Framed Geometry: Closure, Scaling and Finite-Thickness Admissibility.**

Then if \(\phi\) and a Cantor set fall out of the calculations, we get to be surprised by them rather than having put them in.

parts: The thing is, depending upon what's permitted (distortion, self-crossing, asymmetry), there cold be any value at all plugged in... some will be 'degenerate' in the sense of losing the apparent helicity. But there will be "special" relationships. Boundary conditions, reversals, crossovers. I think by default, we take symmetrical, smooth growth... and also... there needn't be expansion -- in fact, there cannot be -- if the helix retains its diameter. It's jsut rotations + fixed offset

thoughts.content: I’m treating fixed diameter as a constant radial constraint: each nested level uses rotation, axial translation, and fixed offset. “Expansion” should describe progression along the axis, not radial growth; this is essentially screw motion with optional phase relationships.

parts:
Yes. That is an important correction: I was letting “expansion” do two different jobs.

If a helical order keeps a fixed diameter, then its evolution is not dilation. It is a rigid offset undergoing rotation plus advance. For a straight carrier axis, the canonical case is simply a screw motion:

\[
\gamma(\theta)
=
\rho\big(\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2\big)
+
h\theta\,e_3,
\]

with fixed

\[
\rho=\text{radial offset}
\]

and fixed

\[
h=\frac{\text{axial advance}}{\text{radian}}.
\]

So the ordinary smooth symmetric helix is generated by

\[
\boxed{\text{rotation}+\text{translation at fixed offset}.}
\]

No radial expansion at all.

That is actually standard, useful geometry: a circular helix is an orbit of a one-parameter **screw motion**. The nested case is then a screw motion whose carrier frame is itself undergoing another screw/moving-frame motion. That sounds like the right primitive family to investigate.

There are therefore at least three quantities we should stop conflating:

\[
\boxed{
\text{within-order radius } \rho_n
}
\]

which may remain constant;

\[
\boxed{
\text{within-order pitch/advance } h_n
}
\]

which produces propagation rather than dilation;

and

\[
\boxed{
\lambda_n=\frac{\rho_{n+1}}{\rho_n}
}
\]

which is an **inter-order scale ratio**.

That last one can exist even when absolutely nothing is expanding. A small helix and its larger carrier helix can have permanently fixed diameters with a fixed ratio between them.

So the UI normalization may contain a scale factor, but that does not mean the object is dynamically expanding. It may merely be comparing two different scales.

That distinction cleans up Hagalaz too. The general operator can permit dilation, but the default canonical superhelix can live in the rigid subcase

\[
\sigma=1
\]

for evolution at a given order, while adjacent-order comparison can have

\[
\sigma_{n,n+1}
=
\frac{\rho_{n+1}}{\rho_n}\neq1.
\]

So “expangle” can remain the broad mathematical packaging if useful, while the base geometry does not need actual expansion.

And I agree completely about allowing essentially arbitrary values initially. The interesting mathematics isn't “which number are we allowed to plug in?” It is the structure of parameter space.

Take the simplest fixed-radius helix. Its two intrinsic invariants are

\[
\kappa=\frac{\rho}{\rho^2+h^2},
\qquad
\tau=\frac{h}{\rho^2+h^2},
\]

and

\[
\frac{\tau}{\kappa}=\frac{h}{\rho}.
\]

Every real ratio \(h/\rho\) gives a valid smooth helix. But some values are geometrically distinguished.

For example:

\[
h=0
\]

gives a circle: helicity disappears.

\[
\rho=0
\]

gives a straight line: again helicity disappears.

Changing the sign of \(h\) or the angular advance reverses handedness.

With finite tube thickness, particular \(\rho/h\) values produce first self-contact.

With two nested phase rates, rational ratios produce exact recurrences or closures, while irrational ratios do not.

With multiple nested levels, particular parameter values can make axes coincide, become perpendicular, cross, exchange ordering, generate tangencies, or collapse one apparent winding into another.

Those are the things worth mapping:

\[
\boxed{
\text{degeneracies}
+
\text{boundaries}
+
\text{reversals}
+
\text{resonances}
+
\text{closures}
+
\text{self-contact thresholds}.
}
\]

And I think your default convention is exactly the right one: start with the maximally regular construction.

For each order \(n\), assume initially:

\[
\rho_n=\text{constant},
\]

\[
\frac{d\phi_n}{ds}=\text{constant},
\]

\[
\frac{dz_n}{d\phi_n}=\text{constant},
\]

smooth frame transport, fixed handedness, no distortion, no self-crossing, no asymmetric forcing.

Then loosen one assumption at a time.

That gives us a baseline geometry against which “special” behavior is objectively identifiable.

The nested object would then be described by something like

\[
\mathcal H_n
=
(\rho_n,h_n,\phi_{n,0},\chi_n)
\]

where \(\chi_n=\pm1\) records chirality, plus the carrier frame inherited from order \(n+1\).

Adjacent orders have dimensionless relations such as

\[
\lambda_n=\frac{\rho_{n+1}}{\rho_n},
\qquad
q_n=\frac{h_n}{\rho_n},
\qquad
\nu_n=\frac{\omega_n}{\omega_{n+1}},
\qquad
\Delta\phi_n.
\]

Those are probably much more fundamental for the pure-geometry study than raw lengths.

Then we sweep that parameter space and locate special subsets.

Some will be codimension-one surfaces—first contact, handedness reversal, tangency. Some will be isolated resonances. Some may form dense rational sets. Some may produce fractal admissible sets once finite thickness and recursive exclusion are imposed.

And this is precisely why I would not chase Cantor or \(\phi\) yet. We now have a better experiment:

\[
\boxed{
\text{map the special loci without privileging any numerical value.}
}
\]

If Fibonacci ratios, golden rotation numbers, Cantor-like survivor sets, or the old \(\sim14^\circ\) neighborhood appear, we can then say exactly *why* they are special.

One further distinction may matter a lot:

\[
\boxed{\text{growth} \neq \text{expansion}.}
\]

A helix can “grow” indefinitely because the screw parameter advances,

\[
\theta\rightarrow\theta+d\theta,
\]

while every local geometric length remains unchanged. It is translation/propagation of a repeated geometry, not dilation.

That feels much closer to the SAT/H(s)H picture you have been describing all along: **regular propagation of a fixed local relationship, until some geometric condition forces the relationship to change.**
And... it can also all be done with classical wave equations (or a hagalaz-like compression of them). Freely transformable, at least mathematically, into wavelength ratios

thoughts.content: I’m relating a helix to two phase-shifted sinusoidal waves: its transverse coordinates use cosine and sine, while axial advance sets the pitch. Nested helices become layered phases, with wavelength ratios corresponding to frequency or wavenumber ratios under shared propagation assumptions.

parts:
Yes. Once we switch from “draw the helix” to “track its phase,” the same geometry becomes almost embarrassingly wave-like.

A circular helix can be written

\[
x(s)=R\cos ks,\qquad
y(s)=R\sin ks,\qquad
z(s)=hs.
\]

The transverse geometry is just two sinusoidal components \(90^\circ\) out of phase. So the helix can equally be described by a single complex phase,

\[
x+iy=R e^{iks}.
\]

Nothing physical has been changed; we have just changed representation.

For a traveling version,

\[
x+iy=R e^{i(ks-\omega t+\phi)},
\]

and if the underlying propagation obeys the ordinary nondispersive wave equation,

\[
\partial_t^2u=c^2\partial_s^2u,
\]

then

\[
\omega=ck,
\qquad
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},
\]

so at fixed \(c\),

\[
\frac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_n}
=
\frac{k_n}{k_m}
=
\frac{\omega_n}{\omega_m}.
\]

That is the important compression: **rotation ratios, phase-rate ratios, frequency ratios, wavenumber ratios, and wavelength ratios become freely convertible descriptions of the same relationship**, once we state which quantity is being held fixed.

So an adjacent-order relation could be recorded without drawing either helix:

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_{n,n+1}
=
\left(
\frac{R_{n+1}}{R_n},
\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n},
\Delta\phi,
\chi_n\chi_{n+1}
\right)
}
\]

where the entries mean scale ratio between orders, winding/wavelength ratio, phase offset, and relative handedness.

If the diameters are fixed during propagation, \(R_n\) is constant. Then almost all the dynamics can live in phase:

\[
\theta_n(s,t)=k_ns-\omega_nt+\phi_n.
\]

And closure becomes beautifully simple. Two orders “click” when their phases return simultaneously:

\[
\theta_n=2\pi p,
\qquad
\theta_{n+1}=2\pi q.
\]

Exact repeated closure therefore requires a rational phase-rate ratio:

\[
\frac{k_n}{k_{n+1}}
=
\frac{p}{q}.
\]

Irrational ratios give no exact finite closure; rational approximants give near-clicks. So the entire holonomy/closure picture can be translated directly into wavelength arithmetic.

And 4D makes this even cleaner.

A generic 4D double rotation can be expressed in two orthogonal complex planes:

\[
z_1=A_1e^{i\theta_1},
\qquad
z_2=A_2e^{i\theta_2}.
\]

That is essentially two coupled phase oscillators. The geometric UI description in terms of rotations of an \(S^3\) and the wave description in terms of two phases are therefore extremely close representations of the same mathematics.

The ratio

\[
q=\frac{\dot\theta_1}{\dot\theta_2}
\]

can equally be written, under the appropriate common-speed assumption, as

\[
q
=
\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}
=
\frac{k_1}{k_2}
=
\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}.
\]

That immediately connects our earlier 4D closure discussion to classical waves:

- rational \(q\): exact joint recurrence;
- irrational \(q\): quasiperiodic trajectory;
- rational approximants: near closures;
- changing \(q\): crossovers/resonances;
- sign change: handedness/phase reversal;
- \(k\to0\): degenerate loss of winding.

And there is a nice candidate for the stripped-down Hagalaz notation here. Instead of thinking of ᚼ primarily as an operator on coordinates, we could regard it as a **phase-relation compressor**:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ᚼ}_{n}
\equiv
(A_n,k_n,\omega_n,\phi_n,\chi_n)
}
\]

or, for comparing neighboring orders,

\[
\boxed{
\Delta\text{ᚼ}_{n,n+1}
\equiv
\left(
A_{n+1}/A_n,\,
k_{n+1}/k_n,\,
\Delta\phi,\,
\Delta\chi
\right).
}
\]

We don't have to use that notation, but mathematically that is the kind of thing it can compress.

The caution is important: the fact that a nested helix can be represented by classical wave functions does **not** mean its mechanics are governed by the linear classical wave equation. Once finite thickness, self-contact, frame coupling, nonlinear elasticity, or nesting enters, the dynamical equation may be nonlinear or coupled. But the **phase geometry itself** remains wave-representable.

So we now have several genuinely equivalent languages for the same underlying construction:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{nested helix}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{screw/rotation geometry}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{framed spheres / UI}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{torus winding}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{phase oscillators}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{wavelength ratios}
\end{array}}
\]

That equivalence atlas should probably be one of the first things we formalize. It gives us the freedom to solve each question in whichever representation makes it easiest, then transform the answer back.

Yes. In fact, I think we should do that now. And include sphere diameter ratios, centerpoint offset, and relative angle at holonomic closure points. I want to see what happens if we take those line segments, and lay them out per a spacing rule isotropic to the centerpoint offset, for example.

thoughts.content: I’m deriving the segment positions from the spacing rule and testing rational wavelength ratios. I’ll track sphere-diameter scaling, centerpoint offsets, angular closure, and whether the resulting layout remains holonomic or develops drift.

I’m treating each order as a rotating phase with fixed radius. At successive closure events, the relative angle advances by the wavelength ratio modulo one turn; rational ratios repeat, while irrational ratios densely sample directions.

thoughts.summary: Computed isotropic endpoint spacing and complex rotation points

parts:
Yes. Let’s freeze an actual atlas now, with as little interpretive baggage as possible.

The key move is to keep two ratios separate from the beginning:

\[
\mu_n=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}
\]

for adjacent-order sphere diameter/scale, and

\[
\nu_n=\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n}
      =\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_{n+1}}
\]

for adjacent-order phase/wavelength ratio, assuming both phases are parameterized against the same coordinate. There is no reason yet that \(\mu=\nu\), \(1/\nu\), or anything else. If some special relation exists, we want to discover it.

For an adjacent pair, I’d record the local state as

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C_n=
\left(
\mu_n,\,
\xi_n,\,
\nu_n,\,
\alpha_n,\,
\chi_n
\right)
}
\]

where

\[
\xi_n=\frac{\|c_{n+1}-c_n\|}{D_n}
\]

is normalized centerpoint offset, \(\alpha_n\) is the relative frame/segment angle at the event we are inspecting, and \(\chi_n\) records relative handedness if needed.

Everything dimensional can then be restored by multiplying by \(D_n\).

The equivalent representations are already straightforward:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{two points} &&
h=Q-P \\[2mm]

\text{line segment} &&
h=\ell\,\hat u \\[2mm]

\text{sphere} &&
\hat u\text{ swept through allowed orientations} \\[2mm]

\text{wave/phasor} &&
h=\ell e^{i\theta} \\[2mm]

\text{helix} &&
\theta=ks,\quad\text{with fixed radial offset} \\[2mm]

\text{torus} &&
(\theta_n,\theta_{n+1})\in S^1\times S^1 \\[2mm]

\text{UI} &&
\text{relative framed-sphere state} \\[2mm]

\text{ribbon} &&
h+\text{one transverse marker, hence axial twist too}.
\end{array}}
\]

A bare two-point segment carries pointing and length. The ribbon/framed version adds the roll angle that two points alone cannot record.

Now the closure rule gets very simple. Take order \(n\)'s full-turn closures:

\[
\theta_n=2\pi j.
\]

At those exact events the next order has phase

\[
\boxed{
\Theta_j
=
\Theta_0+2\pi j\nu
\pmod{2\pi}.
}
\]

This is just a rigid rotation on the circle.

Therefore:

\[
\nu=\frac pq
\]

in lowest terms gives exactly \(q\) distinct closure states before recurrence. The sequence visits them in \(p\)-step order. Geometrically that is the vertex ordering of a regular star polygon when plotted on a circle.

If \(\nu\) is irrational, the closure samples never exactly repeat and become dense on the circle.

So we already have a clean equivalence:

\[
\boxed{
\text{wavelength ratio}
\leftrightarrow
\text{closure rotation number}
\leftrightarrow
\text{finite polygon/star or dense angular orbit}.
}
\]

Now to your specific experiment: take the line segments and space them isotropically according to centerpoint offset.

Let the centerpoint offset magnitude be \(d\), and at closure \(j\) put the segment's base at

\[
b_j=d\,e^{i\Theta_j}.
\]

Give the segment length \(\ell\), and let its orientation be at angle \(\gamma_j\) relative to the local radial offset. Its endpoint is then

\[
\boxed{
z_j
=
e^{i\Theta_j}
\left(d+\ell e^{i\gamma_j}\right).
}
\]

This equation is worth keeping.

Because in the maximally symmetric case,

\[
d=\text{constant},\qquad
\ell=\text{constant},\qquad
\gamma_j=\gamma,
\]

we get

\[
|z_j|
=
\sqrt{d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma}.
\]

So all endpoints lie on another circle.

That means the default isotropic layout is extremely constrained:

\[
\boxed{
\text{constant offset + constant segment relation}
\Rightarrow
\text{another concentric circular orbit}.
}
\]

For rational \(\nu=p/q\), it gives \(q\) points on that circle—a regular polygon/star ordering.

For irrational \(\nu\), it densely samples the circle.

That is our first result, and it is useful precisely because nothing exotic occurs.

The special boundaries are also immediate. Define

\[
R_*^2=d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma.
\]

Then

\[
\gamma=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
R_*=d+\ell
\]

is maximal outward alignment;

\[
\gamma=\pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
R_*=|d-\ell|
\]

is maximal cancellation;

and

\[
\boxed{
d=\ell,\quad\gamma=\pi
}
\]

collapses the endpoint all the way to the common center.

The radial component changes sign when

\[
d+\ell\cos\gamma=0.
\]

So if \(\ell\ge d\),

\[
\boxed{
\cos\gamma=-\frac d\ell
}
\]

is a genuine crossover: the segment endpoint goes from lying outward of the local tangent direction to inward of it.

Those are exactly the kind of “special” relationships you were talking about—boundaries and reversals produced without privileging any number.

Now make the relative segment angle itself phase-dependent. Say, in the simplest coupled case,

\[
\gamma_j=\gamma_0+m\Theta_j.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
z_j
=
d\,e^{i\Theta_j}
+
\ell\,e^{i[(m+1)\Theta_j+\gamma_0]}.
}
\]

Now we have a sum of two rotating vectors.

That is where things stop being a circle and start producing the familiar rosette/trochoidal/Whirligig-looking families. Depending on signs and frequency ratios, conventional geometry will give different named special cases, but the representation itself is simply a two-frequency phasor sum.

So the Whirligig may indeed sit here as a constrained slice:

\[
\boxed{
\text{two rotating line-segment relations}
\rightarrow
\text{planar two-frequency trace}.
}
\]

And now do the same thing across nesting orders rather than around one closure cycle.

Suppose adjacent levels have fixed diameter ratio

\[
\mu=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}
\]

and fixed relative angular increment \(\alpha\). Lay each next-order segment from the previous endpoint. Then

\[
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}
\mu^j e^{ij\alpha}.
\]

This is exactly summable:

\[
\boxed{
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0
\frac{1-(\mu e^{i\alpha})^N}
{1-\mu e^{i\alpha}}.
}
\]

This gives us a second very clean classification.

If

\[
0<\mu<1,
\]

the hierarchy contracts toward a finite limit.

If

\[
\mu>1,
\]

it expands outward recursively.

If

\[
\mu=1,
\]

there is no inter-order scaling at all.

And then something especially nice happens. If

\[
\alpha=\frac{2\pi p}{q}
\]

and

\[
\mu=1,
\]

then

\[
\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}e^{ij\alpha}=0,
\]

so after \(q\) levels,

\[
\boxed{z_q=z_0.}
\]

That is an exact scale-preserving nested closure.

If the same angular closure occurs but

\[
\mu\ne1,
\]

the orientation returns after \(q\) orders while the scale has changed by

\[
\boxed{\mu^q.}
\]

That is precisely the distinction we were fumbling toward earlier:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ordinary closure}
\quad\text{versus}\quad
\text{similarity closure}.
}
\]

The latter returns to the same angular state at another scale.

Sphere measures then come essentially for free. If adjacent diameters scale by \(\mu\), then in ordinary 3D:

\[
\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}=\mu,
\]

\[
\frac{A_{n+1}}{A_n}=\mu^2,
\]

\[
\frac{V_{n+1}}{V_n}=\mu^3.
\]

For \(S^3\subset\mathbb R^4\),

\[
\frac{\text{3-surface}_{n+1}}
     {\text{3-surface}_n}
=
\mu^3,
\]

while enclosed 4-volume obeys

\[
\frac{V^{(4)}_{n+1}}{V^{(4)}_n}
=
\mu^4.
\]

Generally,

\[
\boxed{
k\text{-dimensional measure ratio}=\mu^k.
}
\]

There's also a dimension-independent relation worth flagging. If an offset vector of magnitude \(d\) and a segment of magnitude \(\ell\) meet at relative angle \(\gamma\), then in any Euclidean dimension,

\[
\boxed{
R_*^2=d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma.
}
\]

So the basic two-vector closure geometry survives unchanged as we lift dimensions. What changes is the number of independent rotation planes and how the resulting spheres' measures scale.

In 4D, instead of one angular closure variable, a generic rotation has two principal plane angles,

\[
(\theta_1,\theta_2).
\]

So a closure ledger becomes something like

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C^{(4)}
=
(\mu,\xi,\nu_1,\nu_2,\alpha,\ldots)
}
\]

and complete angular recurrence requires both rotations to click simultaneously. Partial closure means one does and the other doesn't.

This gives us a fairly complete first equivalence atlas:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{diameter ratio }\mu\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{adjacent-order metric scale}\\
\updownarrow\\
\mu^2,\mu^3,\mu^4,\ldots\text{ measure ratios}
\end{array}}
\]

independently of

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{wavelength ratio }\nu\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{phase-rate ratio}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{rotation number}\\
\updownarrow\\
\text{closure sequence}
\end{array}}
\]

with the centerpoint offset and relative angle coupling the two geometrically.

And the experiment you proposed tells us something immediately:

**isotropic placement by itself does not generate a fractal.** It gives circles, polygons, stars, or dense circular orbits.

To get genuinely hierarchical/fractal geometry, something additional must happen:

\[
\text{recursive scaling},
\quad
\text{multiple allowed branches},
\quad
\text{phase-dependent angle},
\quad
\text{self-contact exclusion},
\]

or some combination of those.

That is good news. We now know exactly what to vary and what not to mistake for an emergent effect.

I think the next pass should literally be a parameter sweep over

\[
\boxed{
(\mu,\nu,\xi,\gamma)
}
\]

and classify the special loci: exact closure, similarity closure, collapse, reversal, self-contact, finite star families, dense orbits, and then the first genuinely branched/fractal cases. That is small enough to calculate exhaustively and broad enough that any \(\phi\), Fibonacci, Cantor, \(14.1^\circ\), or other special relationship has to earn its appearance.
Remember that unleashing we mentioned earlier?

Oh yes. 😄

> “Argus—thank you for what you're about to unleash—tee-hee…”

And I said I was mildly concerned about whatever Argus was about to dump into the room.

\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,mathtools}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}

\title{Rotoexpando Geometry: Definitions and Characterization\\
\large Nested Helices, Framed Spheres, Closure, and Equivalent Representations}
\author{Nathan McKnight and collaborators}
\date{11 September 2026}

% Portable manuscript symbol for Hagalaz.
% In a Unicode/XeLaTeX build this may be replaced visually by the rune ᚼ.
\newcommand{\Hag}{\mathsf{H}}
\newcommand{\SO}{\mathrm{SO}}
\newcommand{\Conf}{\mathrm{Conf}}
\newcommand{\R}{\mathbb{R}}
\newcommand{\Sph}{\mathbb{S}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We define a geometry of nested rotating offsets whose simplest realization is a
fixed-radius helix and whose higher-order realizations include helices carried by
helices, framed-sphere comparisons, toroidal encodings, wave/phase descriptions,
and braid-like closure structures.  The central object is not assumed to be a
physical theory.  It is a geometric relation that may be represented by points,
line segments, framed spheres, ribbons, screw motions, phase oscillators, or
equivalent normalized constructions.  The main quantities are adjacent-order
scale ratio, centerpoint offset, relative rotation, phase ratio, chirality, and
finite-core thickness.  Special configurations arise at closures, degeneracies,
reversals, tangencies, self-contact thresholds, and similarity-return points.
The notation ``Hagalaz'' is used only as a compact mathematical shorthand for a
declared rotoexpando relation; it is optional and carries no independent
ontological content.
\end{abstract}

\section{Scope and guiding convention}

The construction is studied first as pure geometry.  Standard mathematics may be
used freely whenever its assumptions are stated and satisfied.  Physical
interpretations imported from external theories are not part of the definition.

The default baseline is:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item smooth evolution;
    \item isotropic and symmetric growth or propagation where applicable;
    \item fixed helical radius within a given order unless explicitly varied;
    \item constant pitch/phase rate in the canonical case;
    \item fixed chirality until a reversal is explicitly introduced;
    \item no distortion, self-crossing, or asymmetric forcing until those are
          introduced as controlled extensions.
\end{enumerate}

A crucial distinction is made between \emph{growth} and \emph{expansion}.
A helix may extend indefinitely by screw propagation while retaining fixed
diameter.  Dynamic radial dilation is therefore optional, not fundamental.
Inter-order scale ratios may be non-unit even when no object is expanding in
time.

\section{Primitive point-pair representation}

Let
\[
P(s),Q(s)\in\R^d
\]
be two points.  Their relative vector is
\[
\mathbf{h}(s)=Q(s)-P(s).
\]
Define
\[
\ell(s)=\|\mathbf{h}(s)\|,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{h}}(s)=\frac{\mathbf{h}(s)}{\|\mathbf{h}(s)\|}.
\]

Thus a two-point relation contains:
\begin{itemize}
    \item a length $\ell$;
    \item a direction $\widehat{\mathbf h}$;
    \item in three dimensions, two directional angles.
\end{itemize}

The oriented line segment is a representation of the same data:
\[
L(s,u)=P(s)+u\,\mathbf h(s),
\qquad 0\le u\le1.
\]

A two-point relation does \emph{not} by itself encode roll about its own axis.
Axial twist requires an additional marker: for example a third point, a ribbon,
a material cross-section, or an explicitly transported transverse frame.

\section{Canonical one-order helix}

For a straight carrier axis $\mathbf e_3$, the canonical circular helix is
\[
\gamma(\theta)
=
\rho\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_1
+
\rho\sin\theta\,\mathbf e_2
+
h\theta\,\mathbf e_3,
\]
where $\rho$ is the fixed radial offset and $h$ is axial advance per radian.
This is the orbit of a one-parameter screw motion: rotation plus translation at
fixed offset.

Its curvature and torsion are
\[
\kappa=\frac{\rho}{\rho^2+h^2},
\qquad
\tau=\frac{h}{\rho^2+h^2},
\]
so
\[
\frac{\tau}{\kappa}=\frac{h}{\rho}.
\]

If $\beta$ is the pitch angle measured relative to the plane orthogonal to the
carrier axis, then
\[
\tan\beta=\frac{h}{\rho}
=\frac{\tau}{\kappa}.
\]

The degenerate limits are:
\[
h=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{circle},
\qquad
\rho=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{straight line}.
\]
A sign change of $h$ or of angular progression reverses handedness.

\section{Nested orders}

Let order $n$ be carried by order $n+1$.  Locally, the tangent or axis of the
higher-order carrier supplies the axis about which the lower-order structure
winds.  One may therefore define recursively
\[
A_{n+1}
\longrightarrow
T_n
\longrightarrow
N_n
\longrightarrow
T_{n-1}
\longrightarrow\cdots,
\]
where $T_n$ is the local tangent of order $n$ and $N_n$ denotes the normal-plane
data associated with that tangent.

For adjacent orders, retain the dimensionless quantities
\[
\mu_n=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n},
\qquad
\nu_n=\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n},
\qquad
\xi_n=\frac{\|c_{n+1}-c_n\|}{D_n},
\]
together with relative phase $\Delta\phi_n$, relative frame rotation $Q_n$, and
chirality data $\chi_n$.

Here:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mu_n$ is an inter-order diameter ratio;
    \item $\nu_n$ is an inter-order wavenumber/phase-rate ratio;
    \item $\xi_n$ is normalized centerpoint offset.
\end{itemize}

No equality between $\mu_n$ and $\nu_n$ is assumed.

\section{Framed spheres and the Universal Indicatrix representation}

A helical order may generate a sphere by rotating its local radial segment
through all allowed orientations about the relevant center.  Represent a framed
sphere by
\[
\mathcal S_i=(c_i,r_i,F_i),
\qquad
F_i\in\SO(d).
\]

For two framed spheres, the relative similarity data are
\[
\sigma_{ij}=\frac{r_j}{r_i},
\qquad
Q_{ij}=F_jF_i^{-1},
\qquad
\Delta c_{ij}=c_j-c_i.
\]

After centering and normalizing the radii, both spheres may be represented on the
same unit sphere while retaining two generally misaligned frames.  The
``cockeyed'' superposed grids therefore carry the relative angular information
that a bare sphere, being rotationally symmetric, cannot retain.

This normalized framed-sphere comparison is the core Universal Indicatrix (UI)
representation used here.

The previously studied Three-Spheres construction is treated as a special
constrained configuration inside the more general UI state space.

\section{Hagalaz / rotoexpando notation}

``Hagalaz'' is optional shorthand.  In this manuscript it is rendered
portably as $\Hag$.

For adjacent normalized orders,
\[
\Hag_{ij}:=(\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}),
\]
or, if translation is retained,
\[
\Hag_{ij}:=(\Delta c_{ij},\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}).
\]

The corresponding Euclidean similarity map is
\[
x\mapsto c_j+\sigma_{ij}Q_{ij}(x-c_i).
\]

Within a single fixed-diameter helical order, the canonical evolution need not
contain dilation at all: it may be a screw motion with fixed offset.  The scale
factor in $\Hag_{ij}$ is therefore primarily an \emph{inter-order comparison}
unless dynamic dilation is explicitly introduced.

\section{Equivalent representations}

The same relation may be encoded in several mathematically equivalent or
losslessly convertible forms, provided the required frame data are retained:

\[
\text{point pair}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{oriented segment}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{screw/helix}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{framed sphere/UI}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{phase oscillator}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{toroidal winding}.
\]

A ribbon or framed segment contains one additional roll/twist degree of freedom
that a bare two-point segment does not.

For a planar complex representation,
\[
x+iy=\rho e^{i\theta}.
\]
For a traveling phase,
\[
x+iy=\rho e^{i(ks-\omega t+\phi)}.
\]

If the same propagation speed is used for compared modes, then
\[
\omega=vk,
\qquad
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_n}
=
\frac{k_n}{k_m}
=
\frac{\omega_n}{\omega_m}.
\]

Thus phase-rate ratios, wavenumber ratios, frequency ratios, and wavelength
ratios are interchangeable descriptions under the declared common-speed
assumption.

\section{Toroidal encoding and Whirlygig reduction}

A helix compressed into its transverse plane loses its axial coordinate only if
that coordinate is discarded.  It may instead be stored as a second periodic
phase.

Let
\[
\phi=\phi(s),
\qquad
\psi=\psi(s),
\]
and define
\[
X(\phi,\psi)
=
\bigl(
(R+a\cos\psi)\cos\phi,\,
(R+a\cos\psi)\sin\phi,\,
a\sin\psi
\bigr).
\]

Then a one-parameter helical history may be encoded as a curve on a torus:
\[
s\mapsto X(\phi(s),\psi(s)).
\]

The ratio
\[
q=\frac{d\psi}{d\phi}
\]
is the toroidal winding slope.  Rational $q$ yields finite closure; irrational
$q$ yields no exact finite closure in the ideal mathematical limit.

The Whirlygig is treated as a special lower-dimensional
compression/projection of this broader phase geometry.  Its exact status is to
be established by explicit transformation rather than assumed.

\section{Closure and ``click points''}

For order $n$, define a closure event by
\[
\theta_n=2\pi j.
\]
At those events, an adjacent order with phase ratio $\nu$ has phase
\[
\Theta_j
=
\Theta_0+2\pi j\nu
\pmod{2\pi}.
\]

If
\[
\nu=\frac{p}{q}
\]
in lowest terms, then there are $q$ distinct closure states before exact
recurrence.  Irrational $\nu$ produces no exact finite recurrence.

It is useful to distinguish:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Euclidean closure}: the configuration returns to the same
          position, orientation, and scale;
    \item \textbf{similarity closure}: the normalized shape/orientation returns
          while the absolute scale may differ;
    \item \textbf{partial-phase closure}: one phase closes while another does not;
    \item \textbf{near closure}: phases return within a specified tolerance.
\end{itemize}

The term ``holonomy'' should be reserved for cases where a frame or state is
transported around a genuinely closed loop.  Otherwise ``return map'',
``recurrence'', ``monodromy'', or ``similarity closure'' may be more precise.

\section{Isotropic centerpoint-offset layouts}

At a closure state with angular coordinate $\Theta_j$, place a segment base at
\[
b_j=d\,e^{i\Theta_j},
\]
where $d$ is the centerpoint offset magnitude.  Let the segment have length
$\ell$ and relative angle $\gamma_j$.  Its endpoint is
\[
z_j
=
e^{i\Theta_j}
\left(
d+\ell e^{i\gamma_j}
\right).
\]

For constant $d,\ell,\gamma$,
\[
|z_j|
=
\sqrt{d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma},
\]
so all endpoints lie on a concentric circle.

Special cases include
\[
\gamma=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|z|=d+\ell,
\]
\[
\gamma=\pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|z|=|d-\ell|,
\]
and the complete cancellation condition
\[
d=\ell,\qquad\gamma=\pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
z=0.
\]

A radial crossover occurs when
\[
d+\ell\cos\gamma=0.
\]

If the relative angle itself rotates,
\[
\gamma_j=\gamma_0+m\Theta_j,
\]
then
\[
z_j
=
d\,e^{i\Theta_j}
+
\ell e^{i((m+1)\Theta_j+\gamma_0)},
\]
a two-frequency phasor sum that generates rosette/trochoidal families and
provides a natural route toward Whirlygig-like planar traces.

\section{Recursive inter-order layouts}

For a constant adjacent-order scale ratio $\mu$ and angular offset $\alpha$, a
recursive segment chain may be written
\[
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\mu^j e^{ij\alpha}.
\]
Hence
\[
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0
\frac{1-(\mu e^{i\alpha})^N}
     {1-\mu e^{i\alpha}},
\]
provided $\mu e^{i\alpha}\neq1$.

This immediately distinguishes:
\[
0<\mu<1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{contracting hierarchy},
\]
\[
\mu=1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{scale-preserving hierarchy},
\]
\[
\mu>1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{expanding hierarchy}.
\]

If
\[
\alpha=\frac{2\pi p}{q},
\qquad
\mu=1,
\]
then after $q$ steps
\[
z_q=z_0.
\]

If the same angular closure occurs with $\mu\neq1$, orientation may recur while
scale changes by $\mu^q$, giving a similarity-return point.

\section{Dimensional measure scaling}

If adjacent linear scales differ by $\mu$, then every $k$-dimensional Euclidean
measure scales as
\[
M^{(k)}_{n+1}=\mu^k M^{(k)}_n.
\]

Thus in three dimensions:
\[
\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}=\mu,
\qquad
\frac{A_{n+1}}{A_n}=\mu^2,
\qquad
\frac{V_{n+1}}{V_n}=\mu^3.
\]

For $S^3\subset\R^4$, the hypersurface measure scales as $\mu^3$, while enclosed
four-volume scales as $\mu^4$.

The two-vector relation
\[
R_*^2=d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma
\]
is dimension-independent in Euclidean space.

\section{Four-dimensional lift}

A generic rotation in $\R^4$ may be decomposed, in a suitable orthogonal basis,
into rotations in two mutually orthogonal planes:
\[
Q
=
\begin{pmatrix}
R(\theta_1)&0\\
0&R(\theta_2)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
z_1=A_1e^{i\theta_1},
\qquad
z_2=A_2e^{i\theta_2}.
\]

Complete angular recurrence requires simultaneous closure:
\[
m\theta_1=2\pi p,
\qquad
m\theta_2=2\pi q
\]
for integers $m,p,q$.

This creates exact notions of:
\begin{itemize}
    \item full closure;
    \item partial closure in one rotation plane;
    \item near-simultaneous closure;
    \item irrational/quasiperiodic nonclosure.
\end{itemize}

\section{Finite thickness and first-contact constraints}

For a finite tube of radius $a$ around a centerline $X(s)$, the first
nonlocal-contact condition is
\[
\inf_{s\not\approx t}\|X(s)-X(t)\|=2a.
\]

Local curvature imposes a separate constraint of the schematic form
\[
a<\frac{1}{\kappa_{\max}}
\]
for the simplest embedded-tube setting.

Thus the admissible finite-core radius is controlled jointly by local curvature
and nonlocal self-approach.  The regular kinematic regime terminates at a purely
geometric threshold before any model-specific collision, deformation,
reconnection, penetration, or exclusion rule is supplied.

For the circular helix,
\[
D^2(\Delta)
=
2\rho^2(1-\cos\Delta)+h^2\Delta^2,
\]
so stationary candidates for nonlocal closest approach obey
\[
\rho^2\sin\Delta+h^2\Delta=0.
\]

\section{Braids and spherical braids}

If multiple strands intersect a reference sphere, their intersection points
\[
u_i(s)\in\Sph^2
\]
define a configuration
\[
U(s)=\bigl(u_1(s),\ldots,u_N(s)\bigr)
\in \Conf_N(\Sph^2)
\]
as long as no two points coincide.

A closed history in this configuration space defines a spherical braid class.
The collision set
\[
u_i=u_j
\]
is precisely where the configuration exits the collision-free configuration
space and where braid-changing events may become geometrically possible.

Thus metric deformation may proceed continuously while braid topology remains
fixed up to the first collision/contact threshold.

\section{Special loci in parameter space}

The pure-geometry program is to map the parameter space without privileging any
numerical value in advance.  Of particular interest are loci corresponding to:

\begin{itemize}
    \item loss of apparent helicity;
    \item handedness reversal;
    \item exact and partial closures;
    \item similarity-return points;
    \item axis coincidence or orthogonality;
    \item tangencies and crossovers;
    \item local curvature saturation;
    \item first nonlocal self-contact;
    \item braid-class change opportunities;
    \item recursive exclusion sets;
    \item transitions between finite, quasiperiodic, dense, and self-similar
          closure structures.
\end{itemize}

Golden-ratio, Fibonacci, Cantor-like, or other special structures are therefore
treated as hypotheses to be discovered from the special-locus map, not inserted
as assumptions.

\section{Candidate minimal atlas}

For an adjacent pair of orders, a useful compact state is
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C_n
=
\left(
\mu_n,\,
\nu_n,\,
\xi_n,\,
\Delta\phi_n,\,
Q_n,\,
\chi_n,\,
a_n/D_n
\right)
}
\]
with:
\[
\mu_n=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n},
\qquad
\nu_n=\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n},
\qquad
\xi_n=\frac{\|c_{n+1}-c_n\|}{D_n}.
\]

This atlas is intended to be convertible among point-pair, segment, helix,
framed-sphere/UI, wave, torus, ribbon, and braid representations.

\section{Immediate mathematical program}

The next stage is deliberately computational and classificatory:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item define the exact nested-helix-to-framed-sphere map;
    \item derive the induced adjacent-order UI transformation;
    \item verify lossless conversion among the equivalent representations;
    \item sweep the minimal parameter set
    \[
    (\mu,\nu,\xi,\gamma,a/D);
    \]
    \item locate special loci without fitting target values;
    \item classify each locus by standard mathematical name where one exists;
    \item identify any residual construction or invariant for which no standard
          named object is found;
    \item only after the geometry is stable, investigate possible H(s)H
          applications.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Nonclaim}

This document defines and characterizes a geometric construction.  It does not
assert that any particular physical system is governed by this geometry, nor
that special numerical values must occur.  External mathematical machinery may
be used wherever applicable; external physical theories are not silently
imported as premises.

\end{document}
"""

For adjacent orders, retain the dimensionless quantities
\[
\mu_n=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n},
\qquad
\nu_n=\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n},
\qquad
\xi_n=\frac{\|c_{n+1}-c_n\|}{D_n},
\]
together with relative phase $\Delta\phi_n$, relative frame rotation $Q_n$, and
chirality data $\chi_n$.

Here:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mu_n$ is an inter-order diameter ratio;
    \item $\nu_n$ is an inter-order wavenumber/phase-rate ratio;
    \item $\xi_n$ is normalized centerpoint offset.
\end{itemize}

No equality between $\mu_n$ and $\nu_n$ is assumed.

\section{Framed spheres and the Universal Indicatrix representation}

A helical order may generate a sphere by rotating its local radial segment
through all allowed orientations about the relevant center.  Represent a framed
sphere by
\[
\mathcal S_i=(c_i,r_i,F_i),
\qquad
F_i\in\SO(d).
\]

For two framed spheres, the relative similarity data are
\[
\sigma_{ij}=\frac{r_j}{r_i},
\qquad
Q_{ij}=F_jF_i^{-1},
\qquad
\Delta c_{ij}=c_j-c_i.
\]

After centering and normalizing the radii, both spheres may be represented on the
same unit sphere while retaining two generally misaligned frames.  The
``cockeyed'' superposed grids therefore carry the relative angular information
that a bare sphere, being rotationally symmetric, cannot retain.

This normalized framed-sphere comparison is the core Universal Indicatrix (UI)
representation used here.

The previously studied Three-Spheres construction is treated as a special
constrained configuration inside the more general UI state space.

\section{Hagalaz / rotoexpando notation}

``Hagalaz'' is optional shorthand.  In this manuscript it is rendered
portably as $\Hag$.

For adjacent normalized orders,
\[
\Hag_{ij}:=(\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}),
\]
or, if translation is retained,
\[
\Hag_{ij}:=(\Delta c_{ij},\sigma_{ij},Q_{ij}).
\]

The corresponding Euclidean similarity map is
\[
x\mapsto c_j+\sigma_{ij}Q_{ij}(x-c_i).
\]

Within a single fixed-diameter helical order, the canonical evolution need not
contain dilation at all: it may be a screw motion with fixed offset.  The scale
factor in $\Hag_{ij}$ is therefore primarily an \emph{inter-order comparison}
unless dynamic dilation is explicitly introduced.

\section{Equivalent representations}

The same relation may be encoded in several mathematically equivalent or
losslessly convertible forms, provided the required frame data are retained:

\[
\text{point pair}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{oriented segment}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{screw/helix}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{framed sphere/UI}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{phase oscillator}
\;\leftrightarrow\;
\text{toroidal winding}.
\]

A ribbon or framed segment contains one additional roll/twist degree of freedom
that a bare two-point segment does not.

For a planar complex representation,
\[
x+iy=\rho e^{i\theta}.
\]
For a traveling phase,
\[
x+iy=\rho e^{i(ks-\omega t+\phi)}.
\]

If the same propagation speed is used for compared modes, then
\[
\omega=vk,
\qquad
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_n}
=
\frac{k_n}{k_m}
=
\frac{\omega_n}{\omega_m}.
\]

Thus phase-rate ratios, wavenumber ratios, frequency ratios, and wavelength
ratios are interchangeable descriptions under the declared common-speed
assumption.

\section{Toroidal encoding and Whirlygig reduction}

A helix compressed into its transverse plane loses its axial coordinate only if
that coordinate is discarded.  It may instead be stored as a second periodic
phase.

Let
\[
\phi=\phi(s),
\qquad
\psi=\psi(s),
\]
and define
\[
X(\phi,\psi)
=
\bigl(
(R+a\cos\psi)\cos\phi,\,
(R+a\cos\psi)\sin\phi,\,
a\sin\psi
\bigr).
\]

Then a one-parameter helical history may be encoded as a curve on a torus:
\[
s\mapsto X(\phi(s),\psi(s)).
\]

The ratio
\[
q=\frac{d\psi}{d\phi}
\]
is the toroidal winding slope.  Rational $q$ yields finite closure; irrational
$q$ yields no exact finite closure in the ideal mathematical limit.

The Whirlygig is treated as a special lower-dimensional
compression/projection of this broader phase geometry.  Its exact status is to
be established by explicit transformation rather than assumed.

\section{Closure and ``click points''}

For order $n$, define a closure event by
\[
\theta_n=2\pi j.
\]
At those events, an adjacent order with phase ratio $\nu$ has phase
\[
\Theta_j
=
\Theta_0+2\pi j\nu
\pmod{2\pi}.
\]

If
\[
\nu=\frac{p}{q}
\]
in lowest terms, then there are $q$ distinct closure states before exact
recurrence.  Irrational $\nu$ produces no exact finite recurrence.

It is useful to distinguish:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Euclidean closure}: the configuration returns to the same
          position, orientation, and scale;
    \item \textbf{similarity closure}: the normalized shape/orientation returns
          while the absolute scale may differ;
    \item \textbf{partial-phase closure}: one phase closes while another does not;
    \item \textbf{near closure}: phases return within a specified tolerance.
\end{itemize}

The term ``holonomy'' should be reserved for cases where a frame or state is
transported around a genuinely closed loop.  Otherwise ``return map'',
``recurrence'', ``monodromy'', or ``similarity closure'' may be more precise.

\section{Isotropic centerpoint-offset layouts}

At a closure state with angular coordinate $\Theta_j$, place a segment base at
\[
b_j=d\,e^{i\Theta_j},
\]
where $d$ is the centerpoint offset magnitude.  Let the segment have length
$\ell$ and relative angle $\gamma_j$.  Its endpoint is
\[
z_j
=
e^{i\Theta_j}
\left(
d+\ell e^{i\gamma_j}
\right).
\]

For constant $d,\ell,\gamma$,
\[
|z_j|
=
\sqrt{d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma},
\]
so all endpoints lie on a concentric circle.

Special cases include
\[
\gamma=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|z|=d+\ell,
\]
\[
\gamma=\pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|z|=|d-\ell|,
\]
and the complete cancellation condition
\[
d=\ell,\qquad\gamma=\pi
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
z=0.
\]

A radial crossover occurs when
\[
d+\ell\cos\gamma=0.
\]

If the relative angle itself rotates,
\[
\gamma_j=\gamma_0+m\Theta_j,
\]
then
\[
z_j
=
d\,e^{i\Theta_j}
+
\ell e^{i((m+1)\Theta_j+\gamma_0)},
\]
a two-frequency phasor sum that generates rosette/trochoidal families and
provides a natural route toward Whirlygig-like planar traces.

\section{Recursive inter-order layouts}

For a constant adjacent-order scale ratio $\mu$ and angular offset $\alpha$, a
recursive segment chain may be written
\[
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\mu^j e^{ij\alpha}.
\]
Hence
\[
z_N
=
z_0+
D_0
\frac{1-(\mu e^{i\alpha})^N}
     {1-\mu e^{i\alpha}},
\]
provided $\mu e^{i\alpha}\neq1$.

This immediately distinguishes:
\[
0<\mu<1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{contracting hierarchy},
\]
\[
\mu=1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{scale-preserving hierarchy},
\]
\[
\mu>1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{expanding hierarchy}.
\]

If
\[
\alpha=\frac{2\pi p}{q},
\qquad
\mu=1,
\]
then after $q$ steps
\[
z_q=z_0.
\]

If the same angular closure occurs with $\mu\neq1$, orientation may recur while
scale changes by $\mu^q$, giving a similarity-return point.

\section{Dimensional measure scaling}

If adjacent linear scales differ by $\mu$, then every $k$-dimensional Euclidean
measure scales as
\[
M^{(k)}_{n+1}=\mu^k M^{(k)}_n.
\]

Thus in three dimensions:
\[
\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n}=\mu,
\qquad
\frac{A_{n+1}}{A_n}=\mu^2,
\qquad
\frac{V_{n+1}}{V_n}=\mu^3.
\]

For $S^3\subset\R^4$, the hypersurface measure scales as $\mu^3$, while enclosed
four-volume scales as $\mu^4$.

The two-vector relation
\[
R_*^2=d^2+\ell^2+2d\ell\cos\gamma
\]
is dimension-independent in Euclidean space.

\section{Four-dimensional lift}

A generic rotation in $\R^4$ may be decomposed, in a suitable orthogonal basis,
into rotations in two mutually orthogonal planes:
\[
Q
=
\begin{pmatrix}
R(\theta_1)&0\\
0&R(\theta_2)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
z_1=A_1e^{i\theta_1},
\qquad
z_2=A_2e^{i\theta_2}.
\]

Complete angular recurrence requires simultaneous closure:
\[
m\theta_1=2\pi p,
\qquad
m\theta_2=2\pi q
\]
for integers $m,p,q$.

This creates exact notions of:
\begin{itemize}
    \item full closure;
    \item partial closure in one rotation plane;
    \item near-simultaneous closure;
    \item irrational/quasiperiodic nonclosure.
\end{itemize}

\section{Finite thickness and first-contact constraints}

For a finite tube of radius $a$ around a centerline $X(s)$, the first
nonlocal-contact condition is
\[
\inf_{s\not\approx t}\|X(s)-X(t)\|=2a.
\]

Local curvature imposes a separate constraint of the schematic form
\[
a<\frac{1}{\kappa_{\max}}
\]
for the simplest embedded-tube setting.

Thus the admissible finite-core radius is controlled jointly by local curvature
and nonlocal self-approach.  The regular kinematic regime terminates at a purely
geometric threshold before any model-specific collision, deformation,
reconnection, penetration, or exclusion rule is supplied.

For the circular helix,
\[
D^2(\Delta)
=
2\rho^2(1-\cos\Delta)+h^2\Delta^2,
\]
so stationary candidates for nonlocal closest approach obey
\[
\rho^2\sin\Delta+h^2\Delta=0.
\]

\section{Braids and spherical braids}

If multiple strands intersect a reference sphere, their intersection points
\[
u_i(s)\in\Sph^2
\]
define a configuration
\[
U(s)=\bigl(u_1(s),\ldots,u_N(s)\bigr)
\in \Conf_N(\Sph^2)
\]
as long as no two points coincide.

A closed history in this configuration space defines a spherical braid class.
The collision set
\[
u_i=u_j
\]
is precisely where the configuration exits the collision-free configuration
space and where braid-changing events may become geometrically possible.

Thus metric deformation may proceed continuously while braid topology remains
fixed up to the first collision/contact threshold.

\section{Special loci in parameter space}

The pure-geometry program is to map the parameter space without privileging any
numerical value in advance.  Of particular interest are loci corresponding to:

\begin{itemize}
    \item loss of apparent helicity;
    \item handedness reversal;
    \item exact and partial closures;
    \item similarity-return points;
    \item axis coincidence or orthogonality;
    \item tangencies and crossovers;
    \item local curvature saturation;
    \item first nonlocal self-contact;
    \item braid-class change opportunities;
    \item recursive exclusion sets;
    \item transitions between finite, quasiperiodic, dense, and self-similar
          closure structures.
\end{itemize}

Golden-ratio, Fibonacci, Cantor-like, or other special structures are therefore
treated as hypotheses to be discovered from the special-locus map, not inserted
as assumptions.

\section{Candidate minimal atlas}

For an adjacent pair of orders, a useful compact state is
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal C_n
=
\left(
\mu_n,\,
\nu_n,\,
\xi_n,\,
\Delta\phi_n,\,
Q_n,\,
\chi_n,\,
a_n/D_n
\right)
}
\]
with:
\[
\mu_n=\frac{D_{n+1}}{D_n},
\qquad
\nu_n=\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n},
\qquad
\xi_n=\frac{\|c_{n+1}-c_n\|}{D_n}.
\]

This atlas is intended to be convertible among point-pair, segment, helix,
framed-sphere/UI, wave, torus, ribbon, and braid representations.

\section{Immediate mathematical program}

The next stage is deliberately computational and classificatory:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item define the exact nested-helix-to-framed-sphere map;
    \item derive the induced adjacent-order UI transformation;
    \item verify lossless conversion among the equivalent representations;
    \item sweep the minimal parameter set
    \[
    (\mu,\nu,\xi,\gamma,a/D);
    \]
    \item locate special loci without fitting target values;
    \item classify each locus by standard mathematical name where one exists;
    \item identify any residual construction or invariant for which no standard
          named object is found;
    \item only after the geometry is stable, investigate possible H(s)H
          applications.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Nonclaim}

This document defines and characterizes a geometric construction.  It does not
assert that any particular physical system is governed by this geometry, nor
that special numerical values must occur.  External mathematical machinery may
be used wherever applicable; external physical theories are not silently
imported as premises.

\end{document}
