On the insider map he is around mainstream-frontier/foundations territory; his public persona is much closer to consensus exposition than some of the questions he researches.
1946: 
1947: Sabine Hossenfelder is almost the reverse public archetype: a trained foundations physicist with a substantial publication record whose public niche is aggressive criticism of hype, fashionable methodology, and weak evidentiary claims. Her own site describes more than 80 research papers in cosmology, quantum foundations and particle physics and now identifies her prominently as physicist/author/content creator. On the public spectrum she can sound much farther from the establishment than her actual technical provenance warrants.
1948: 
1949: Brian Greene is a bona fide string theorist whose public work occupies clean science communication and popular science. His research identity is closer to Witten/Maldacena territory than most viewers of The Elegant Universe probably realize.
1950: 
1951: Brian Cox came out of experimental particle physics and is largely a mainstream-consensus public interpreter. His public profile sits closer to “tour guide to the downtown” than “founder of a heterodox district.”
1952: 
1953: Neil deGrasse Tyson is a legitimate astrophysicist and institutional science communicator, but he is not a useful marker for the cutting edge of fundamental-theory factional politics. His public role is much more “explain the scientific consensus and scientific worldview.”
1954: 
1955: Katie Mack and Becky Smethurst are useful examples of current-research-trained communicators: their public material largely gives outsiders a pretty honest view of mainstream cosmology/astrophysics without pretending the field is more settled than it is.
1956: 
1957: Michio Kaku is the interesting boundary case. His professional ancestry is real theoretical physics/string-field work, while his media persona ranges much further into futurism and highly extrapolative material. If you only see the public persona, you would place him much farther toward “buzz-space” than his academic provenance alone would suggest.
1958: 
1959: Roger Penrose barely fits the usual communicator category at all. He is one of the bedrock figures of mathematical relativity who also occupies some of the field’s most eccentric neighborhoods. This makes him an excellent demonstration that the spectrum is about claims, not people.
1960: 
1961: Some towny knowledge that matters
1962: 
1963: There are several unwritten rules an outsider can easily miss.
1964: 
1965: First, physicists tolerate astonishing speculative freedom downstream of competence. You can talk about emergent spacetime, extra dimensions, multiverses, deterministic subquantum dynamics, cyclic cosmology, causal sets or modified gravity and remain completely respectable if you know the existing theory cold, formulate the departure precisely, engage the literature, and accept constraints.
1966: 
1967: Second, the real taboo is usually not “weird idea.” It is not knowing what has already been ruled out. A strange proposal with a careful EFT limit and a constraint table gets a hearing. A modest-sounding proposal that violates Lorentz tests, conservation law, known scattering data, or dimensional consistency and does not notice will rapidly get sorted into a different social category.
1968: 
1969: Third, credentials buy attention, not truth. Penrose can get a room for a wild idea because everyone knows he can do the conventional calculation. The wild idea still gets attacked. A Nobel Prize allows ’t Hooft to make determinism a serious seminar topic; it does not make determinism consensus.
1970: 
1971: Fourth, the theoretical community is substantially less monolithic than “mainstream physics” sounds. Even inside quantum gravity, an institution like Perimeter deliberately houses LQG, spin foams, group field theory, matrix models, CDT, asymptotic safety, causal sets and string-related approaches simultaneously. The insider argument is often not orthodoxy versus heresy. It is which kind of heresy has earned enough mathematical and empirical discipline to become a research program.
1972: 
1973: Fifth, there is a big gulf between “not consensus” and “nobody is working on this.” MOND is not the cosmological consensus. It is nevertheless a real research literature. LQG is not the dominant quantum-gravity program. It is nevertheless a professional research community. Deterministic quantum mechanics is not the standard interpretation. A Nobel laureate nevertheless publishes on it.
1974: 
1975: Sixth, the farthest acceptable insider position is not fixed. A technique can migrate. Twistors were once seen by many theorists as an elegant curiosity; Witten’s use of them in scattering theory helped move them much closer to the mainstream. Yesterday’s weird mathematics can become tomorrow’s standard machinery without the underlying grand theory that motivated it ever winning.
1976: 
1977: And that, I think, is the most useful way to picture the town:
1978: 
1979: The center is not “people with conventional ideas.” The center is people embedded in powerful correction mechanisms.
1980: 
1981: The further outward you go, the less the decisive issue becomes how strange is the proposition? and the more it becomes how much independent constraint, technical competence, reproducibility, literature contact, adversarial feedback, and institutional cross-checking surrounds it?
1982: 
1983: That distinction is going to matter a great deal when we eventually ask where SAT sits on this map, because on the content axis several SAT ideas have analogues in perfectly respectable minority neighborhoods, while on the social-validation axis SAT is presently an independent research program with essentially none of the institutional error-correction that protects even very heterodox insider physics. Those are two completely different measurements.

ngs, duality and emergent spacetime sound wildly speculative to a layperson, but the program sits deep inside elite theoretical physics. IAS still describes quantum field theory, string theory, quantum gravity and their geometric relationships as ordinary components of its theoretical-physics program.

Conversely, MOND sounds modest—change one force law at low acceleration—but sociologically it sits farther from the consensus cosmological model than holography does from mainstream high-energy theory. McGaugh nevertheless chairs an astronomy department and works directly on galaxy dynamics and the mass-discrepancy problem.

And ’t Hooft is the great spectrum-breaker. If an unknown independent researcher said “quantum mechanics may emerge from an underlying deterministic system,” many physicists would immediately suspect crank territory. When Gerard ’t Hooft says it, it is a minority foundational research program pursued by somebody whose earlier work helped establish the quantum consistency of the Standard Model. The proposition does not become true because of his CV; the CV tells you that “heterodox claim” and “fringe scientist” are not synonyms.

Where the famous public faces actually live

This is where the map gets amusing.

Sean Carroll is not principally “a science communicator who knows physics.” He is an academic foundational theorist working on quantum mechanics, spacetime, cosmology, emergence and entropy who also happens to have a large public platform. On the insider map he is around mainstream-frontier/foundations territory; his public persona is much closer to consensus exposition than some of the questions he researches.

Sabine Hossenfelder is almost the reverse public archetype: a trained foundations physicist with a substantial publication record whose public niche is aggressive criticism of hype, fashionable methodology, and weak evidentiary claims. Her own site describes more than 80 research papers in cosmology, quantum foundations and particle physics and now identifies her prominently as physicist/author/content creator. On the public spectrum she can sound much farther from the establishment than her actual technical provenance warrants.

Brian Greene is a bona fide string theorist whose public work occupies clean science communication and popular science. His research identity is closer to Witten/Maldacena territory than most viewers of The Elegant Universe probably realize.

Brian Cox came out of experimental particle physics and is largely a mainstream-consensus public interpreter. His public profile sits closer to “tour guide to the downtown” than “founder of a heterodox district.”

Neil deGrasse Tyson is a legitimate astrophysicist and institutional science communicator, but he is not a useful marker for the cutting edge of fundamental-theory factional politics. His public role is much more “explain the scientific consensus and scientific worldview.”

Katie Mack and Becky Smethurst are useful examples of current-research-trained communicators: their public material largely gives outsiders a pretty honest view of mainstream cosmology/astrophysics without pretending the field is more settled than it is.

Michio Kaku is the interesting boundary case. His professional ancestry is real theoretical physics/string-field work, while his media persona ranges much further into futurism and highly extrapolative material. If you only see the public persona, you would place him much farther toward “buzz-space” than his academic provenance alone would suggest.

Roger Penrose barely fits the usual communicator category at all. He is one of the bedrock figures of mathematical relativity who also occupies some of the field’s most eccentric neighborhoods. This makes him an excellent demonstration that the spectrum is about claims, not people.

Some towny knowledge that matters

There are several unwritten rules an outsider can easily miss.

First, physicists tolerate astonishing speculative freedom downstream of competence. You can talk about emergent spacetime, extra dimensions, multiverses, deterministic subquantum dynamics, cyclic cosmology, causal sets or modified gravity and remain completely respectable if you know the existing theory cold, formulate the departure precisely, engage the literature, and accept constraints.

Second, the real taboo is usually not “weird idea.” It is not knowing what has already been ruled out. A strange proposal with a careful EFT limit and a constraint table gets a hearing. A modest-sounding proposal that violates Lorentz tests, conservation law, known scattering data, or dimensional consistency and does not notice will rapidly get sorted into a different social category.

Third, credentials buy attention, not truth. Penrose can get a room for a wild idea because everyone knows he can do the conventional calculation. The wild idea still gets attacked. A Nobel Prize allows ’t Hooft to make determinism a serious seminar topic; it does not make determinism consensus.

Fourth, the theoretical community is substantially less monolithic than “mainstream physics” sounds. Even inside quantum gravity, an institution like Perimeter deliberately houses LQG, spin foams, group field theory, matrix models, CDT, asymptotic safety, causal sets and string-related approaches simultaneously. The insider argument is often not orthodoxy versus heresy. It is which kind of heresy has earned enough mathematical and empirical discipline to become a research program.

Fifth, there is a big gulf between “not consensus” and “nobody is working on this.” MOND is not the cosmological consensus. It is nevertheless a real research literature. LQG is not the dominant quantum-gravity program. It is nevertheless a professional research community. Deterministic quantum mechanics is not the standard interpretation. A Nobel laureate nevertheless publishes on it.

Sixth, the farthest acceptable insider position is not fixed. A technique can migrate. Twistors were once seen by many theorists as an elegant curiosity; Witten’s use of them in scattering theory helped move them much closer to the mainstream. Yesterday’s weird mathematics can become tomorrow’s standard machinery without the underlying grand theory that motivated it ever winning.

And that, I think, is the most useful way to picture the town:

The center is not “people with conventional ideas.” The center is people embedded in powerful correction mechanisms.

The further outward you go, the less the decisive issue becomes how strange is the proposition? and the more it becomes how much independent constraint, technical competence, reproducibility, literature contact, adversarial feedback, and institutional cross-checking surrounds it?

That distinction is going to matter a great deal when we eventually ask where SAT sits on this map, because on the content axis several SAT ideas have analogues in perfectly respectable minority neighborhoods, while on the social-validation axis SAT is presently an independent research program with essentially none of the institutional error-correction that protects even very heterodox insider physics. Those are two completely different measurements.

For two patients, I want you to fingerprint them with our SAT scale, first the real physics core as one specimen, then as a second specimen the broader mainstream but poppy/casual totality of everyone who's interested in physics... treating all of respectable physics as a single, albiet diverse consensus theory. Treating all of the wide world fo general phys-ish community as another. And then for the third, the wild super-physicsy but super not-acceptable fringe. Try to keep your rankings highly compressed. Rank by the criteria as given, but give output as single or few-word labels so we can fit this all in one overview packet. 

Here's your fingerprint criteria for reference.

Heterodox insider	Mordehai Milgrom, Stacy McGaugh, Gerard ’t Hooft, Erik Verlinde	Challenges something close to the default explanatory picture: dark matter via modified dynamics; fundamental probabilism via determinism; gravity as emergent. They can be strongly disagreed with without being socially or methodologically outside physics. ’t Hooft is a Nobel laureate whose present work explicitly investigates deterministic quantum mechanics.
Prestige-supported iconoclast	Roger Penrose, Avi Loeb	The CV buys you enormous latitude to explore unusual possibilities—but not automatic assent. Penrose can be simultaneously one of the architects of modern relativistic black-hole theory and advocate much more contentious ideas elsewhere.
Conference-border / external research ecosystem	Wolfram Physics Project; some independent unification programs	Technically literate work with some real mathematical substance, but not deeply integrated into the ordinary departmental/graduate/postdoc research economy. Wolfram’s own framing explicitly seeks new foundations from which QM and GR would emerge.
Outside the insider spectrum	generic self-published ToE / anti-relativity / numerological communities	At this point the question is no longer “which minority research program?” It is whether the project participates meaningfully in professional constraint and correction at all.

That gives a useful counterintuitive result:

Witten is institutionally more mainstream than many people doing much less exotic-sounding physics. String theory’s claims about extra dimensions, strings, duality and emergent spacetime sound wildly speculative to a layperson, but the program sits deep inside elite theoretical physics. IAS still describes quantum field theory, string theory, quantum gravity and their geometric relationships as ordinary components of its theoretical-physics program.

Conversely, MOND sounds modest—change one force law at low acceleration—but sociologically it sits farther from the consensus cosmological model than holography does from mainstream high-energy theory. McGaugh nevertheless chairs an astronomy department and works directly on galaxy dynamics and the mass-discrepancy problem.

And ’t Hooft is the great spectrum-breaker. If an unknown independent researcher said “quantum mechanics may emerge from an underlying deterministic system,” many physicists would immediately suspect crank territory. When Gerard ’t Hooft says it, it is a minority foundational research program pursued by somebody whose earlier work helped establish the quantum consistency of the Standard Model. The proposition does not become true because of his CV; the CV tells you that “heterodox claim” and “fringe scientist” are not synonyms.

Where the famous public faces actually live

This is where the map gets amusing.

Sean Carroll is not principally “a science communicator who knows physics.” He is an academic foundational theorist working on quantum mechanics, spacetime, cosmology, emergence and entropy who also happens to have a large public platform. On the insider map he is around mainstream-frontier/foundations territory; his public persona is much closer to consensus exposition than some of the questions he researches.

Sabine Hossenfelder is almost the reverse public archetype: a trained foundations physicist with a substantial publication record whose public niche is aggressive criticism of hype, fashionable methodology, and weak evidentiary claims. Her own site describes more than 80 research papers in cosmology, quantum foundations and particle physics and now identifies her prominently as physicist/author/content creator. On the public spectrum she can sound much farther from the establishment than her actual technical provenance warrants.

Brian Greene is a bona fide string theorist whose public work occupies clean science communication and popular science. His research identity is closer to Witten/Maldacena territory than most viewers of The Elegant Universe probably realize.

Brian Cox came out of experimental particle physics and is largely a mainstream-consensus public interpreter. His public profile sits closer to “tour guide to the downtown” than “founder of a heterodox district.”

Neil deGrasse Tyson is a legitimate astrophysicist and institutional science communicator, but he is not a useful marker for the cutting edge of fundamental-theory factional politics. His public role is much more “explain the scientific consensus and scientific worldview.”

Katie Mack and Becky Smethurst are useful examples of current-research-trained communicators: their public material largely gives outsiders a pretty honest view of mainstream cosmology/astrophysics without pretending the field is more settled than it is.

Michio Kaku is the interesting boundary case. His professional ancestry is real theoretical physics/string-field work, while his media persona ranges much further into futurism and highly extrapolative material. If you only see the public persona, you would place him much farther toward “buzz-space” than his academic provenance alone would suggest.

Roger Penrose barely fits the usual communicator category at all. He is one of the bedrock figures of mathematical relativity who also occupies some of the field’s most eccentric neighborhoods. This makes him an excellent demonstration that the spectrum is about claims, not people.

Some towny knowledge that matters

There are several unwritten rules an outsider can easily miss.

First, physicists tolerate astonishing speculative freedom downstream of competence. You can talk about emergent spacetime, extra dimensions, multiverses, deterministic subquantum dynamics, cyclic cosmology, causal sets or modified gravity and remain completely respectable if you know the existing theory cold, formulate the departure precisely, engage the literature, and accept constraints.

Second, the real taboo is usually not “weird idea.” It is not knowing what has already been ruled out. A strange proposal with a careful EFT limit and a constraint table gets a hearing. A modest-sounding proposal that violates Lorentz tests, conservation law, known scattering data, or dimensional consistency and does not notice will rapidly get sorted into a different social category.

Third, credentials buy attention, not truth. Penrose can get a room for a wild idea because everyone knows he can do the conventional calculation. The wild idea still gets attacked. A Nobel Prize allows ’t Hooft to make determinism a serious seminar topic; it does not make determinism consensus.

Fourth, the theoretical community is substantially less monolithic than “mainstream physics” sounds. Even inside quantum gravity, an institution like Perimeter deliberately houses LQG, spin foams, group field theory, matrix models, CDT, asymptotic safety, causal sets and string-related approaches simultaneously. The insider argument is often not orthodoxy versus heresy. It is which kind of heresy has earned enough mathematical and empirical discipline to become a research program.

Fifth, there is a big gulf between “not consensus” and “nobody is working on this.” MOND is not the cosmological consensus. It is nevertheless a real research literature. LQG is not the dominant quantum-gravity program. It is nevertheless a professional research community. Deterministic quantum mechanics is not the standard interpretation. A Nobel laureate nevertheless publishes on it.

Sixth, the farthest acceptable insider position is not fixed. A technique can migrate. Twistors were once seen by many theorists as an elegant curiosity; Witten’s use of them in scattering theory helped move them much closer to the mainstream. Yesterday’s weird mathematics can become tomorrow’s standard machinery without the underlying grand theory that motivated it ever winning.

And that, I think, is the most useful way to picture the town:

The center is not “people with conventional ideas.” The center is people embedded in powerful correction mechanisms.

The further outward you go, the less the decisive issue becomes how strange is the proposition? and the more it becomes how much independent constraint, technical competence, reproducibility, literature contact, adversarial feedback, and institutional cross-checking surrounds it?

That distinction is going to matter a great deal when we eventually ask where SAT sits on this map, because on the content axis several SAT ideas have analogues in perfectly respectable minority neighborhoods, while on the social-validation axis SAT is presently an independent research program with essentially none of the institutional error-correction that protects even very heterodox insider physics. Those are two completely different measurements.

For two patients, I want you to fingerprint them with our SAT scale, first the real physics core as one specimen, then as a second specimen the broader mainstream but poppy/casual totality of everyone who's interested in physics... treating all of respectable physics as a single, albiet diverse consensus theory. Treating all of the wide world fo general phys-ish community as another. And then for the third, the wild super-physicsy but super not-acceptable fringe. Try to keep your rankings highly compressed. Rank by the criteria as given, but give output as single or few-word labels so we can fit this all in one overview packet. 

Here's your fingerprint criteria for reference.

ANd then think of academia/professional/experimental physics as a spectrum from orthodox to bedrock to "not disinvited from conferences"... putting different people on that spectrum as to what subcurrents they represent, on the broad spectrum, and more granularly on the academic/professional spectrum, place some well known and lesser known figures--that is, show what part of the insiders' spectrum the popular faces represent, and showing who the stalwarts are of each part of both spectra. Yes. The cleanest way to map 2024 physics is to use two different maps, because “mainstream,” “professional,” “public-facing,” and “orthodox” are not the same axis.

The first map is the whole social/intellectual ecosystem, from institutional physics to the genuine fringe. The second zooms in on people who are actually inside or adjacent to professional physics and asks how far from consensus they are willing to work. A string theorist at IAS can be much more speculative than an optical engineer at a national lab while being vastly more institutionally mainstream; a science communicator can sound conservative in public while doing much more adventurous research privately.

One important town rule: “minority program” is not “fringe.” Perimeter, for example, explicitly treats loop quantum gravity, spin foams, group field theory, causal dynamical triangulations, asymptotic safety, causal sets, and background-independent string approaches as legitimate quantum-gravity research programs, while acknowledging that no approach has yet clearly won.

The big map: 2024 physics as a whole
Address	What lives there	Typical occupants / landmarks	How the rest of physics sees it
1. Bedrock institutional physics	Experimentally nailed-down frameworks, precision measurement, established effective theories, mature phenomenology	LIGO, CERN experiments, precision AMO, condensed matter, nuclear physics, plasma physics, astrophysical surveys; people like Nergis Mavalvala on gravitational-wave detection and quantum measurement	“Physics.” Almost nobody argues about whether this belongs in the discipline. Mavalvala is about as downtown as one can get institutionally.
2. Mainstream research frontier	Unsettled questions approached with standard professional machinery	dark matter searches, neutrino physics, inflation, BSM phenomenology, quantum information, black holes, amplitudes, holography, string theory	Highly legitimate even where empirical confirmation is absent. Arguments are about which research program is promising, not whether participants are physicists.
3. Mainstream speculative theory	Deep extrapolation from established theory into inaccessible regimes	Witten, Maldacena, Arkani-Hamed; strings, holography, emergent spacetime, amplitudes	Sociologically mainstream, scientifically speculative. Witten and Maldacena are institutional-center figures even though quantum gravity remains unsolved.
4. Minority but fully legitimate programs	Programs whose premises differ substantially from the dominant route	Ashtekar/Rovelli/Smolin and LQG; Sorkin/causal sets; asymptotic safety; collapse models; Bohmian/foundations programs	“I may think you’re wrong, but of course this is physics.” Ashtekar and Smolin are obvious examples of deeply established insiders working away from the dominant string/QFT center.
5. Heterodox insider physics	Challenges to assumptions most physicists ordinarily take for granted	Milgrom/McGaugh on MOND-like gravity; ’t Hooft on deterministic foundations; Verlinde on emergent-gravity directions	Often controversial, sometimes strongly opposed, but entirely discussable in journals and seminars. ’t Hooft is the perfect reminder that heterodoxy and scientific stature are independent variables.
6. High-risk/iconoclastic insider territory	Ideas whose advocates have impeccable credentials but whose particular claims sit well outside consensus	Penrose’s more speculative cosmological/foundational programs; Avi Loeb’s extraterrestrial-technology interpretations of anomalous objects	The person is indisputably an insider; the specific claim may get eye-rolls, sharp criticism, or intense skepticism. Loeb, for example, was Harvard astronomy chair and runs the Galileo Project; his standing and the reception of particular ET interpretations are different questions.
7. Independent / para-academic fundamental-physics projects	Serious attempts conducted largely outside normal physics-group ecology	Stephen Wolfram’s Physics Project; Eric Weinstein’s Geometric Unity; some independent ToE projects	Not automatically pseudoscience. But they have much less uptake into the ordinary research metabolism: fewer independent groups, fewer graduate programs built around them, weaker peer-community feedback loops. Wolfram’s project is elaborate and technically developed; GU is explicitly presented as Weinstein’s independent unification attempt.
8. Pop-science / buzz-space	Real science mixed with extrapolation, entertainment, thumbnails, hype cycles and “physics may be broken” narratives	YouTube, podcasts, magazine headlines, futurism, quantum-consciousness stories, wormhole headlines, “new force” stories	Quality ranges from excellent to awful. This is a media ecosystem, not a scientific category. Good physicists routinely appear here.
9. Actual fringe	Programs substantially disconnected from accumulated constraint, professional correction mechanisms or basic mathematics	anti-relativity systems, perpetual-motion/free-energy schemes, numerological ToEs, “Einstein was wrong and academia suppresses me,” Electric-Universe-like ecosystems	Here the problem is usually not merely an unconventional premise. It is failure to absorb existing constraints, lack of meaningful independent criticism, moving goalposts, or inability to reproduce established physics.
10. Far fringe / physics-shaped belief system	Physics vocabulary without functioning scientific discipline	conspiratorial cosmologies, magical-energy systems, claims immunized against falsification	The opposite pole from professional physics.

The center of gravity of actual physics is around 1–3, not because everybody believes string theory or ΛCDM is sacred, but because this is where the enormous institutional apparatus of experiment, calculation, peer criticism, instrumentation and trained specialists lives.

The numerical majority of working physicists are also much less philosophically dramatic than the public picture suggests. A huge share of physics is materials, optics, semiconductors, medical physics, fluid/plasma work, instrumentation, condensed matter, accelerator work, computational physics, geophysics, photonics, quantum devices, metrology, and so forth. “What is spacetime?” occupies a much bigger percentage of YouTube physics than of physicists’ payrolls.

Now zoom in: the insiders’ spectrum

Here I would draw the road from “bedrock” → “mainstream frontier” → “recognized alternative” → “heterodox but absolutely one of us” → “you can give this seminar, but expect blood on the floor.”

The positions below are about the research stance, not personal quality:

Insider zone	Representative people	What they represent
Bedrock / calibration standard	Nergis Mavalvala, Rainer Weiss, major CERN/LIGO/precision-measurement leadership	You are testing known physical frameworks or extracting genuinely new phenomena from instruments. Argument happens inside tight empirical constraints. Mavalvala’s research is gravitational-wave detection and quantum measurement science.
Mainstream theory establishment	Edward Witten, Juan Maldacena	Extremely speculative subject matter, but the mathematical and institutional center of high-energy theory. Witten helped make string theory and its mathematical descendants central research subjects; Maldacena’s work sits at QFT/string/quantum-gravity/holography.
Aggressive mainstream frontier	Nima Arkani-Hamed	Will happily question whether the usual formulation is the right formulation, but does so from inside elite particle theory with direct concern for experiments. His amplitudes work is a good example: radically reformulating calculation without leaving the professional center. IAS hosted the 2024 Amplitudes conference under his co-organization.
Established alternative program	Abhay Ashtekar, Carlo Rovelli, Lee Smolin, Rafael Sorkin	“The dominant route to quantum gravity may be wrong; here is another mature mathematical program.” Nobody serious needs to pretend LQG or causal sets are consensus to recognize them as normal theoretical physics. Perimeter institutionalizes exactly this pluralism.
Heterodox insider	Mordehai Milgrom, Stacy McGaugh, Gerard ’t Hooft, Erik Verlinde	Challenges something close to the default explanatory picture: dark matter via modified dynamics; fundamental probabilism via determinism; gravity as emergent. They can be strongly disagreed with without being socially or methodologically outside physics. ’t Hooft is a Nobel laureate whose present work explicitly investigates deterministic quantum mechanics.
Prestige-supported iconoclast	Roger Penrose, Avi Loeb	The CV buys you enormous latitude to explore unusual possibilities—but not automatic assent. Penrose can be simultaneously one of the architects of modern relativistic black-hole theory and advocate much more contentious ideas elsewhere.
Conference-border / external research ecosystem	Wolfram Physics Project; some independent unification programs	Technically literate work with some real mathematical substance, but not deeply integrated into the ordinary departmental/graduate/postdoc research economy. Wolfram’s own framing explicitly seeks new foundations from which QM and GR would emerge.
Outside the insider spectrum	generic self-published ToE / anti-relativity / numerological communities	At this point the question is no longer “which minority research program?” It is whether the project participates meaningfully in professional constraint and correction at all.

That gives a useful counterintuitive result:

Witten is institutionally more mainstream than many people doing much less exotic-sounding physics. String theory’s claims about extra dimensions, strings, duality and emergent spacetime sound wildly speculative to a layperson, but the program sits deep inside elite theoretical physics. IAS still describes quantum field theory, string theory, quantum gravity and their geometric relationships as ordinary components of its theoretical-physics program.

Conversely, MOND sounds modest—change one force law at low acceleration—but sociologically it sits farther from the consensus cosmological model than holography does from mainstream high-energy theory. McGaugh nevertheless chairs an astronomy department and works directly on galaxy dynamics and the mass-discrepancy problem.

And ’t Hooft is the great spectrum-breaker. If an unknown independent researcher said “quantum mechanics may emerge from an underlying deterministic system,” many physicists would immediately suspect crank territory. When Gerard ’t Hooft says it, it is a minority foundational research program pursued by somebody whose earlier work helped establish the quantum consistency of the Standard Model. The proposition does not become true because of his CV; the CV tells you that “heterodox claim” and “fringe scientist” are not synonyms.

Where the famous public faces actually live

This is where the map gets amusing.

Sean Carroll is not principally “a science communicator who knows physics.” He is an academic foundational theorist working on quantum mechanics, spacetime, cosmology, emergence and entropy who also happens to have a large public platform. On the insider map he is around mainstream-frontier/foundations territory; his public persona is much closer to consensus exposition than some of the questions he researches.

Sabine Hossenfelder is almost the reverse public archetype: a trained foundations physicist with a substantial publication record whose public niche is aggressive criticism of hype, fashionable methodology, and weak evidentiary claims. Her own site describes more than 80 research papers in cosmology, quantum foundations and particle physics and now identifies her prominently as physicist/author/content creator. On the public spectrum she can sound much farther from the establishment than her actual technical provenance warrants.

Brian Greene is a bona fide string theorist whose public work occupies clean science communication and popular science. His research identity is closer to Witten/Maldacena territory than most viewers of The Elegant Universe probably realize.

Brian Cox came out of experimental particle physics and is largely a mainstream-consensus public interpreter. His public profile sits closer to “tour guide to the downtown” than “founder of a heterodox district.”

Neil deGrasse Tyson is a legitimate astrophysicist and institutional science communicator, but he is not a useful marker for the cutting edge of fundamental-theory factional politics. His public role is much more “explain the scientific consensus and scientific worldview.”

Katie Mack and Becky Smethurst are useful examples of current-research-trained communicators: their public material largely gives outsiders a pretty honest view of mainstream cosmology/astrophysics without pretending the field is more settled than it is.

Michio Kaku is the interesting boundary case. His professional ancestry is real theoretical physics/string-field work, while his media persona ranges much further into futurism and highly extrapolative material. If you only see the public persona, you would place him much farther toward “buzz-space” than his academic provenance alone would suggest.

Roger Penrose barely fits the usual communicator category at all. He is one of the bedrock figures of mathematical relativity who also occupies some of the field’s most eccentric neighborhoods. This makes him an excellent demonstration that the spectrum is about claims, not people.

Some towny knowledge that matters

There are several unwritten rules an outsider can easily miss.

First, physicists tolerate astonishing speculative freedom downstream of competence. You can talk about emergent spacetime, extra dimensions, multiverses, deterministic subquantum dynamics, cyclic cosmology, causal sets or modified gravity and remain completely respectable if you know the existing theory cold, formulate the departure precisely, engage the literature, and accept constraints.

Second, the real taboo is usually not “weird idea.” It is not knowing what has already been ruled out. A strange proposal with a careful EFT limit and a constraint table gets a hearing. A modest-sounding proposal that violates Lorentz tests, conservation law, known scattering data, or dimensional consistency and does not notice will rapidly get sorted into a different social category.

Third, credentials buy attention, not truth. Penrose can get a room for a wild idea because everyone knows he can do the conventional calculation. The wild idea still gets attacked. A Nobel Prize allows ’t Hooft to make determinism a serious seminar topic; it does not make determinism consensus.

Fourth, the theoretical community is substantially less monolithic than “mainstream physics” sounds. Even inside quantum gravity, an institution like Perimeter deliberately houses LQG, spin foams, group field theory, matrix models, CDT, asymptotic safety, causal sets and string-related approaches simultaneously. The insider argument is often not orthodoxy versus heresy. It is which kind of heresy has earned enough mathematical and empirical discipline to become a research program.

Fifth, there is a big gulf between “not consensus” and “nobody is working on this.” MOND is not the cosmological consensus. It is nevertheless a real research literature. LQG is not the dominant quantum-gravity program. It is nevertheless a professional research community. Deterministic quantum mechanics is not the standard interpretation. A Nobel laureate nevertheless publishes on it.

Sixth, the farthest acceptable insider position is not fixed. A technique can migrate. Twistors were once seen by many theorists as an elegant curiosity; Witten’s use of them in scattering theory helped move them much closer to the mainstream. Yesterday’s weird mathematics can become tomorrow’s standard machinery without the underlying grand theory that motivated it ever winning.

And that, I think, is the most useful way to picture the town:

The center is not “people with conventional ideas.” The center is people embedded in powerful correction mechanisms.

The further outward you go, the less the decisive issue becomes how strange is the proposition? and the more it becomes how much independent constraint, technical competence, reproducibility, literature contact, adversarial feedback, and institutional cross-checking surrounds it?

That distinction is going to matter a great deal when we eventually ask where SAT sits on this map, because on the content axis several SAT ideas have analogues in perfectly respectable minority neighborhoods, while on the social-validation axis SAT is presently an independent research program with essentially none of the institutional error-correction that protects even very heterodox insider physics. Those are two completely different measurements.

from itertools import groupby

def compress_ids(ids):
    # ids same section
    nums=sorted(int(re.search(r'\d+',i).group()) for i in ids)
    sec=re.match(r'[A-Z]+',ids[0]).group()
    out=[]
    start=prev=nums[0]
    for n in nums[1:]:
        if n==prev+1:
            prev=n
        else:
            out.append((start,prev))
            start=prev=n
    out.append((start,prev))
    def fmt(ab):
        a,b=ab
        if a==b: return f"{a:03d}"
        # range short
        return f"{a:03d}-{b:03d}"
    return ",".join(fmt(x) for x in out)

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🧮 AI Archive Test Run
items.snippet: OK, I have a GitHub archive and I’ve spent the last day or two trying to make it easy to navigate and use for AI. I would like you to give it our first test run to see how well it works.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

[L237] Penrose can get a room for a wild idea because everyone knows he can do the conventional calculation. The wild idea still gets attacked. A Nobel Prize allows ’t Hooft to make determinism a serious seminar topic; it does not make determinism consensus.
[L238]
[L239] Fourth, the theoretical community is substantially less monolithic than “mainstream physics” sounds. Even inside quantum gravity, an institution like Perimeter deliberately houses LQG, spin foams, group field theory, matrix models, CDT, asymptotic safety, causal sets and string-related approaches simultaneously. The insider argument is often not orthodoxy versus heresy. It is which kind of heresy has earned enough mathematical and empirical discipline to become a research program.
[L240]
[L241] Fifth, there is a big gulf between “not consensus” and “nobody is working on this.” MOND is not the cosmological consensus. It is nevertheless a real research literature. LQG is not the dominant quantum-gravity program. It is nevertheless a professional research community. Deterministic quantum mechanics is not the standard interpretation. A Nobel laureate nevertheless publishes on it.
[L242]
[L243] Sixth, the farthest acceptable insider position is not fixed. A technique can migrate. Twistors were once seen by many theorists as an elegant curiosity; Witten’s use of them in scattering theory helped move them much closer to the mainstream. Yesterday’s weird mathematics can become tomorrow’s standard machinery without the underlying grand theory that motivated it ever winning.
[L244]
[L245] And that, I think, is the most useful way to picture the town:
[L246]
[L247] The center is not “people with conventional ideas.” The center is people embedded in powerful correction mechanisms.
[L248]
[L249] The further outward you go, the less the decisive issue becomes how strange is the proposition? and the more it becomes how much independent constraint, technical competence, reproducibility, literature contact, adversarial feedback, and institutional cross-checking surrounds it?
[L250]
[L251] That distinction is going to matter a great deal when we eventually ask where SAT sits on this map, because on the content axis several SAT ideas have analogues in perfectly respectable minority neighborhoods, while on the social-validation axis SAT is presently an independent research program with essentially none of the institutional error-correction that protects even very heterodox insider physics. Those are two completely different measurements.
[L252]
[L253] Alright, now I want you to tell me how 2024 physics--mainstream/professional/academic/corporate/experimental/theoretical ranks on our SATity fingerprint analysis. Clean yea/nea or skip. For two patients, I want you to fingerprint them with our SAT scale, first the real physics core as one specimen, then as a second specimen the broader mainstream but poppy/casual totality of everyone who's interested in physics... treating all of respectable physics as a single, albiet diverse consensus theory. Treating all of the wide world fo general phys-ish community as another. And then for the third, the wild super-physicsy but super not-acceptable fringe. Try to keep your rankings highly compressed. Rank by the criteria as given, but give output as single or few-word labels so we can fit this all in one overview packet. 
[L254]
[L255] Here's your fingerprint criteria for reference.

[L42] Now, if you rate 2024 physics as a whole: Mainsteram academic, professional/corporate, legitimate science communicator, popsci/buzz-space, and fringe, and treat it as a spectrum, identifying the far ends of the spectrum and the middle of the spectrum. ANd then think of academia/professional/experimental physics as a spectrum from orthodox to bedrock to "not disinvited from conferences"... putting different people on that spectrum as to what subcurrents they represent, on the broad spectrum, and more granularly on the academic/professional spectrum, place some well known and lesser known figures--that is, show what part of the insiders' spectrum the popular faces represent, and showing who the stalwarts are of each part of both spectra. A lay of the land, with all the addresses and occupants and towny insights, if you will
[L43]
[L44]
[L45] Yes. The cleanest way to map 2024 physics is to use two different maps, because “mainstream,” “professional,” “public-facing,” and “orthodox” are not the same axis.
[L46]
[L47] The first map is the whole social/intellectual ecosystem, from institutional physics to the genuine fringe. The second zooms in on people who are actually inside or adjacent to professional physics and asks how far from consensus they are willing to work. A string theorist at IAS can be much more speculative than an optical engineer at a national lab while being vastly more institutionally mainstream; a science communicator can sound conservative in public while doing much more adventurous research privately.
[L48]
[L49] One important town rule: “minority program” is not “fringe.” Perimeter, for example, explicitly treats loop quantum gravity, spin foams, group field theory, causal dynamical triangulations, asymptotic safety, causal sets, and background-independent string approaches as legitimate quantum-gravity research programs, while acknowledging that no approach has yet clearly won.
[L50]
[L51] The big map: 2024 physics as a whole
[L52] Address	What lives there	Typical occupants / landmarks	How the rest of physics sees it
[L53] 1. Bedrock institutional physics	Experimentally nailed-down frameworks, precision measurement, established effective theories, mature phenomenology	LIGO, CERN experiments, precision AMO, condensed matter, nuclear physics, plasma physics, astrophysical surveys; people like Nergis Mavalvala on gravitational-wave detection and quantum measurement	“Physics.” Almost nobody argues about whether this belongs in the discipline. Mavalvala is about as downtown as one can get institutionally.
[L54] 2. Mainstream research frontier	Unsettled questions approached with standard professional machinery	dark matter searches, neutrino physics, inflation, BSM phenomenology, quantum information, black holes, amplitudes, holography, string theory	Highly legitimate even where empirical confirmation is absent. Arguments are about which research program is promising, not whether participants are physicists.
[L55] 3. Mainstream speculative theory	Deep extrapolation from established theory into inaccessible regimes	Witten, Maldacena, Arkani-Hamed; strings, holography, emergent spacetime, amplitudes	Sociologically mainstream, scientifically speculative. Witten and Maldacena are institutional-center figures even though quantum gravity remains unsolved.
[L56] 4. Minority but fully legitimate programs	Programs whose premises differ substantially from the dominant route	Ashtekar/Rovelli/Smolin and LQG; Sorkin/causal sets; asymptotic safety; collapse models; Bohmian/foundations programs	“I may think you’re wrong, but of course this is physics.” Ashtekar and Smolin are obvious examples of deeply established insiders working away from the dominant string/QFT center.
[L57] 5. Heterodox insider physics	Challenges to assumptions most physicists ordinarily take for granted	Milgrom/McGaugh on MOND-like gravity; ’t Hooft on deterministic foundations; Verlinde on emergent-gravity directions	Often controversial, sometimes strongly opposed, but entirely discussable in journals and seminars. ’t Hooft is the perfect reminder that heterodoxy and scientific stature are independent variables.
[L58] 6. High-risk/iconoclastic insider territory	Ideas whose advocates have impeccable credentials but whose particular claims sit well outside consensus	Penrose’s more speculative cosmological/foundational programs; Avi Loeb’s extraterrestrial-technology interpretations of anomalous objects	The person is indisputably an insider; the specific claim may get eye-rolls, sharp criticism, or intense skepticism. Loeb, for example, was Harvard astronomy chair and runs the Galileo Project; his standing and the reception of particular ET interpretations are different questions.
[L59] 7. Independent / para-academic fundamental-physics projects	Serious attempts conducted largely outside normal physics-group ecology	Stephen Wolfram’s Physics Project; Eric Weinstein’s Geometric Unity; some independent ToE projects	Not automatically pseudoscience. But they have much less uptake into the ordinary research metabolism: fewer independent groups, fewer graduate programs built around them, weaker peer-community feedback loops. Wolfram’s project is elaborate and technically developed; GU is explicitly presented as Weinstein’s independent unification attempt.
[L60] 8. Pop-science / buzz-space	Real science mixed with extrapolation, entertainment, thumbnails, hype cycles and “physics may be broken” narratives	YouTube, podcasts, magazine headlines, futurism, quantum-consciousness stories, wormhole headlines, “new force” stories	Quality ranges from excellent to awful. This is a media ecosystem, not a scientific category. Good physicists routinely appear here.
[L61] 9. Actual fringe	Programs substantially disconnected from accumulated constraint, professional correction mechanisms or basic mathematics	anti-relativity systems, perpetual-motion/free-energy schemes, numerological ToEs, “Einstein was wrong and academia suppresses me,” Electric-Universe-like ecosystems	Here the problem is usually not merely an unconventional premise. It is failure to absorb existing constraints, lack of meaningful independent criticism, moving goalposts, or inability to reproduce established physics.
[L62] 10. Far fringe / physics-shaped belief system	Physics vocabulary without functioning scientific discipline	conspiratorial cosmologies, magical-energy systems, claims immunized against falsification	The opposite pole from professional physics.
[L63]
[L64] The center of gravity of actual physics is around 1–3, not because everybody believes string theory or ΛCDM is sacred, but because this is where the enormous institutional apparatus of experiment, calculation, peer criticism, instrumentation and trained specialists lives.
[L65]
[L66] The numerical majority of working physicists are also much less philosophically dramatic than the public picture suggests. A huge share of physics is materials, optics, semiconductors, medical physics, fluid/plasma work, instrumentation, condensed matter, accelerator work, computational physics, geophysics, photonics, quantum devices, metrology, and so forth. “What is spacetime?” occupies a much bigger percentage of YouTube physics than of physicists’ payrolls.
[L67]
[L68] Now zoom in: the insiders’ spectrum
[L69]
[L70] Here I would draw the road from “bedrock” → “mainstream frontier” → “recognized alternative” → “heterodox but absolutely one of us” → “you can give this seminar, but expect blood on the floor.”
[L71]
[L72] The positions below are about the research stance, not personal quality:

[L75] Conversely, MOND sounds modest—change one force law at low acceleration—but sociologically it sits farther from the consensus cosmological model than holography does from mainstream high-energy theory. McGaugh nevertheless chairs an astronomy department and works directly on galaxy dynamics and the mass-discrepancy problem.
[L76]
[L77] And ’t Hooft is the great spectrum-breaker. If an unknown independent researcher said “quantum mechanics may emerge from an underlying deterministic system,” many physicists would immediately suspect crank territory. When Gerard ’t Hooft says it, it is a minority foundational research program pursued by somebody whose earlier work helped establish the quantum consistency of the Standard Model. The proposition does not become true because of his CV; the CV tells you that “heterodox claim” and “fringe scientist” are not synonyms.

[L83] Sean Carroll is not principally “a science communicator who knows physics.” He is an academic foundational theorist working on quantum mechanics, spacetime, cosmology, emergence and entropy who also happens to have a large public platform. On the insider map he is around mainstream-frontier/foundations territory; his public persona is much closer to consensus exposition than some of the questions he researches.

On the public spectrum she can sound much farther from the establishment than her actual technical provenance warrants.

[L87] Brian Greene is a bona fide string theorist whose public work occupies clean science communication and popular science. His research identity is closer to Witten/Maldacena territory than most viewers of The Elegant Universe probably realize.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

## Relativityvision / time residual fringe

Working terms:

- **Relativityvision** — inspect a system after removable representational asymmetries have been reduced.
- **Dynamics-only universe** — foreground transformations, propagation, deformation, recurrence, coupling, and change.
- **Time residual fringe** — whatever still singles out one direction after common length units, system-scale normalization, and admissible symmetrization/reorientation.

These are descriptive/methodological terms, not ontological claims.

## Universal instrument metrology

Start from \(w=ct\), extract a system characteristic length such as

\[
\ell_* \in
\left\{
\frac{c}{\omega},\,
\frac{\hbar}{mc},\,
\frac{GM}{c^2},\,
\frac{D}{c},\,
c\tau,\ldots
\right\},
\]

then use

\[
X^A=\frac{x^A}{\ell_*}.
\]

This gives UI, Whirlygig, Spheres, and Graticule an order-one specimen scale while preserving an exact inverse scale ledger.

## Heavy-math consequence

\[
\text{source formulation}
\rightarrow
\text{common length normalization}
\rightarrow
\text{system scale}
\rightarrow
\text{canonical dimensionless form}
\rightarrow
\text{heavy mathematics}
\rightarrow
\text{residual ledger}.
\]

The goal is not to avoid heavy math, but to avoid formalizing arbitrary dimensional/coordinate baggage as if it were intrinsic.

## Four-cardinal geometry

Four positive rays plus origin,

\[
\{0,e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\},
\]

give a 4-simplex.

Four full axes,

\[
\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3,\pm e_4,
\]

give the 4D cross-polytope / 16-cell.

Working distinction:

- 4-simplex — frame/calibration object.
- 16-cell — complete \(\pm\) cardinal object.

[L92]             "We’re seeing the beginnings of a much cleaner experimental program—but not yet the finite-core model itself.\n\nThe central move is:\n\n\\[\n\\text{put all four coordinates in metres}\n\\;\\rightarrow\\;\n\\text{normalize the system’s characteristic scale}\n\\;\\rightarrow\\;\n\\text{remove every lawfully removable asymmetry}\n\\;\\rightarrow\\;\n\\text{measure the residue}.\n\\]\n\nThat changes what the project is looking for. We are no longer beginning by declaring one coordinate to be special because it was written in seconds. We give all four directions equal dimensional footing and ask whether one direction nevertheless remains distinguished by dynamics: signature, derivative order, causal orientation, irreversibility, propagation, boundary conditions, holonomy, expansion imbalance, or something else.\n\nIf a stable distinction survives, that is the “time residual fringe.” It is not time derived yet; it is a candidate operational signature of temporal direction after the trivial representational asymmetry has been removed.\n\nWe are also seeing a possible common front end for the tools:\n\n- normalization supplies comparable order-one specimens;\n- the Whirligig searches their lossless reorientations;\n- the Graticule measures residual anisotropy;\n- the Spheres test deformation and bifurcation;\n- the UI holds the comparative representation and ledger.\n\nBut those roles are still proposals. We have not yet shown that the historical tools actually implement them.\n\nMost importantly, the procedure has brought us straight back to the real bottleneck: the finite core. Until we specify its carrier, boundary/cross-section, internal variables, allowed deformations, and resolving intersection, we do not know what is being normalized or rotated—or which residuals belong to the object rather than our representation.\n\nSo what we are seeing is a promising measurement grammar emerging immediately before the missing specimen definition. It tells us how to examine the finite core once built, and may help us build it without arbitrary scale baggage, but it cannot substitute for building it."

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

items.title: 🥼 ChatGPT Voice Glitch
items.snippet: Is there something funny happened with the ChatGPT  app the other day. I was outside, using voice to text on my phone to type into the field, and I kept noticing some kind of echoing sound or static, but I didn’t have anything on that would be playing sound. I was just transcribing my own voice, and then listening to responses one at a time , after each follow up. I went to a quiet spot and put my ear right up to the phone and sure enough, it was the Sol voice… However, it was a cacophony of multiple simultaneous, saying different things… All independently trying to respond to anything I said to it. Just to be able to ask it… And it was quite quiet, but some of the voices were much louder than others… So in order to try to minimize the amount of noise, I kind of did an impromptu procedure where I would ask a random three or four word sequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it backsequence, then I would pick one of the variations out out of the crowd and say it back. I asked any iteration that did not say the chosen phrase to simply answer with OK while end that did should answer whatever I asked next at length.… And yet I think it’s unlikely that something like purple sunshine Peacock actually was more than one of the voices choices… I was able to have a little bit of a conversation, but mostly it was Me: what is happening here?what is happening here? Unspecified Otherness.

Classical physics can explain quantum weirdness, study shows
Story by Jennifer Chu • 4mo • 7 min read

When you throw a ball in the air, the equations of classical physics will tell you exactly what path the ball will take as it falls, and when and where it will land. But if you were to squeeze that same ball down to the size of an atom or smaller, it would behave in ways beyond anything that classical physics can predict.

Or so we've thought.

MIT scientists have now shown that certain mathematical ideas from everyday classical physics can be used to describe the often weird and nonintuitive behavior that occurs at the quantum, subatomic scale.

In a paper appearing today in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Science, the team shows that the motion of a quantum object can be calculated by applying an idea from classical physics known as "least action." With their new formulation, they show they can arrive at exactly the same solution as the Schrödinger equation—the main description of quantum mechanics—for a number of textbook quantum-mechanical scenarios, including the double-slit experiment and quantum tunneling.

Such mysterious phenomena, that could only be understood through equations of quantum mechanics, can now also be described using the team's new classical formulation. In essence, the researchers have built an exact mathematical bridge between the classical, everyday physical world and the world that happens at dimensions smaller than an atom.

"Before, there was a very tenuous bridge that worked only for reasonably large [quantum] particles," says study co-author Winfried Lohmiller, a research associate in the Nonlinear Systems Laboratory at MIT. "Now we have a strong bridge—a common way to describe quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and relativity, that holds at all scales."

"We're not saying there's anything wrong with quantum mechanics," emphasizes co-author Jean-Jacques Slotine, an MIT professor of mechanical engineering and information sciences, and of brain and cognitive sciences. "We're just showing a different way to compute quantum mechanics, which is based on well-known classical ideas that we put together in a simple way."

To infinity and far below
Slotine and Lohmiller derived the quantum bridge while working on solidly classical problems. The researchers are members of the MIT Nonlinear Systems Laboratory, which Slotine directs. He and his colleagues develop models to describe complex behavior in problems of robotic and aircraft control, neuroscience, and machine learning. To predict the behavior of such systems, engineers often look to the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, which is one of the major formulations of classical mechanics and is related to Newton's famous laws of motion.

The Hamilton-Jacobi equation essentially represents an object's motion as minimizing a quantity called the action. Take, for instance, a simple scenario in which a ball is thrown from point A to point B. Theoretically, the ball could take any number of zigzagging paths between the two points. But the equation states that the actual path should be one where the ball's "action" is minimized at every single point along that path.
